docs.title: About the Blueye Drones
docs.text:
Blueye makes the Pioneer, Pro, X1, X3, X3 Ultra and X7 underwater drones, and the SDK works with all of them. The Pioneer and Pro are built for inspection. The other models have guest ports for tools such as grippers, sonars and positioning systems, and the X3 Ultra and X7 add a 4K camera and can run computer vision models on the drone.

Model Camera Camera tilt Guest ports CV models Pioneer Up to 1080p None None No Pro Up to 1080p ±30° None No X1 Up to 1080p ±30° 1 No X3 Up to 1080p ±30° 3 No X3 Ultra 4K ±30° 3 Yes X7 4K ±90° 6 Yes

See Blueye drone models for the differences that matter to a script, and blueyerobotics.com for more about the drones.

docs.title: This SDK and the Blueye drones
docs.text:
A Blueye drone is normally controlled via a mobile device through the Blueye App (iOS/Android). The mobile device is connected via Wi-Fi to a surface unit, and the drone is connected to the surface unit via a tether cable.

This python SDK exposes the functionality of the Blueye app through a Python object. The SDK enables remote control of a Blueye drone as well as reading telemetry data and viewing video streams. It is not meant for executing code on the drone itself.

To control the drone you connect your laptop to the surface unit Wi-Fi and run code that interfaces with the through the Python object.

Check out the Quick Start Guide to get started with using the SDK.

docs.title: The blueye CLI
docs.text:
The SDK ships with a blueye command line interface for working with the drone from the terminal. It is installed together with the SDK:

pip install blueye.sdk

Running blueye --help lists the available commands. Two features need the SDK's cli extra:

  • blueye bundle-model inspects ONNX files and needs the onnx package.
  • blueye logs download --mcap and blueye logs convert write .mcap files and need mcap-protobuf-support.
pip install "blueye.sdk[cli]"

(Keep the quotes — most shells treat square brackets specially.) Everything else works without the extra. When a command needs a package that is missing, it prints the install command for your platform instead of failing with an import error; bundle-model then exits with code 2, the .mcap paths of logs with code 1.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Drone address. Commands that talk to the drone take --drone-ip (default 192.168.1.101) and --timeout in seconds (default 10 for logs, 5 for models). Give them after the action, as in blueye logs list --drone-ip 192.168.1.102; without an action (the interactive session) they follow the command name. bundle-model only contacts the drone with --push and takes --drone-ip for that.

Interactive and scripted use. blueye logs and blueye models run without an action open an interactive session when stdin and stdout are a terminal; piped or redirected, they print the list instead. bundle-model prompts for every value a flag did not supply; --yes accepts the inferred defaults and asks nothing. Every prompt names the flag that answers it.

Exit codes.

Code Meaning 0 Success 1 A user-facing error: the drone could not be reached, a file is missing, invalid metadata, a declined confirmation 2 bundle-model needs the cli extra and it is missing, or the arguments were invalid 130 Interrupted with Ctrl-C

Third-party tools (see below) propagate their own exit code.

docs.title: Bundling CV models — blueye bundle-model
docs.text:
The Blueye X3 Ultra and X7 can run your own computer vision models: object detection, instance segmentation, and single-object tracking. The drone's vision pipeline consumes model packages — a zip containing an ONNX model and a model_meta.json file that describes how to preprocess frames and decode the model's outputs.

The blueye bundle-model command turns an exported ONNX file into such a package. It

  • validates that the model is of a supported type,
  • auto-generates model_meta.json from the ONNX graph and any embedded metadata (Ultralytics exports carry their class names and input size along),
  • interactively asks about anything that cannot be inferred, and
  • writes a deployable zip.

docs.title: Interactive use
docs.text:
Point the command at your ONNX file and answer the prompts:

blueye bundle-model path/to/model.onnx

The CLI inspects the model, shows what it inferred (output format, class count, input size, labels), and walks through the remaining choices with interactive prompts — model name, tracking algorithm, and the runtime configuration for the drone:

  • Execution device — the CLI analyzes the network and recommends the Jetson DLA cores (tensorrt-dla0/tensorrt-dla1) for convolution-style models, which frees the GPU for other work. Models with layers the DLA cannot run (NMS-in-graph, transformers) get tensorrt recommended instead. You can always pick any device.
  • Inference rate — maximum rate in Hz, defaulting to unlimited.
  • Autolaunch — whether the drone should start this model automatically. Defaults to enabled; pass --no-runtime-enabled to bundle the package disabled.
  • Package metadata — a version string (default 1.0.0) plus optional description, author, and license. These are informational fields carried inside model_meta.json so the package stays self-describing wherever it travels (drone web UI, Blueye App, Blueye Cloud). Use an SPDX identifier for the license when you can (MIT, Apache-2.0, AGPL-3.0, Proprietary).

The result is a zip with model.onnx and model_meta.json at its root.

docs.title: Scripted use
docs.text:
Every prompt can be answered with a flag, and --yes accepts all inferred defaults:

blueye bundle-model yolov8n.onnx --yes \
    --name "YOLOv8n (COCO)" \
    --model-version 1.0.0 --author "Ultralytics" --license AGPL-3.0 \
    --description "YOLOv8n nano object detector trained on COCO (80 classes)" \
    --tracking byte_track \
    --runtime-device tensorrt-dla0 --runtime-hz 10 --runtime-enabled \
    --output yolov8n_package.zip

Use --dry-run to print the generated model_meta.json without writing anything, and --labels labels.txt (one class name per line) when the model does not embed its class names.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Package and output:

Option Meaning onnx_path The ONNX file. Prompted for when omitted. --name NAME Human-readable model name. Default: the name embedded in the model, else the file stem. --model-version VERSION Version string written to the metadata. Default 1.0.0. --description, --author, --license Informational package fields. Passing any of them skips the "add package details?" prompt. -o, --output PATH Output zip. Default <name>_package.zip in the current directory. --force Overwrite an existing zip. Without it, interactive runs ask and scripted runs fail. --dry-run Print the generated model_meta.json and stop; nothing is written. --push Upload the zip to the drone after writing it. --drone-ip IP Drone address used by --push. Default 192.168.1.101. -y, --yes Accept every inferred default; never prompt. --strict Treat onnx.checker failures as fatal instead of asking whether to continue. --quiet Print only errors and the result path.

Model structure (all inferred from the ONNX graph when possible):

Option Meaning --format FORMAT Decoder format; one of the values in the table below. Prompted for when inference is uncertain. --labels FILE Class names, one per line. Default: the labels embedded in the model. --num-classes N Number of classes. Default: inferred from the output shape or the label count. --input-size WxH Model input size, e.g. 640x640. Needed when the model has dynamic dimensions. --anchors "W,H W,H ..." Anchor pairs in grid-cell units, yolov2_grid only. --grid-size N Feature-map grid size, yolov2_grid only. Default: inferred, else prompted (13). --one-indexed-classes Class IDs start at 1 (TensorFlow SSD exports), ssd_multi only. --template-size PX, --search-size PX Template and search crop sizes for single-object trackers. Defaults 128/256 (ostrack), 112/224 (mixformerv2).

Preprocessing and decoding:

Option Meaning --color-order {rgb,bgr} Channel order the model expects. Default rgb. --normalize-scale FLOAT Pixel scale. Default 1/255 for most formats, 1.0 for yolov2_grid and ssd_multi. --normalize-mean R,G,B, --normalize-std R,G,B Per-channel normalization. Default: ImageNet values for detr, ostrack and mixformerv2, none otherwise. --confidence-threshold FLOAT Detection confidence threshold, detection packages only. Default 0.3. Trackers keep their package default (0.5). --nms-threshold FLOAT NMS IoU threshold. Default 0.45. --tracking {none,iou,byte_track} Multi-object tracking algorithm for detection packages. Default none.

Runtime configuration on the drone:

Option Meaning --runtime-device DEVICE cuda, tensorrt, tensorrt-dla0 or tensorrt-dla1 on the drone. cpu and coreml are accepted for local desktop testing of the package. --runtime-hz HZ Maximum inference rate in Hz, or max for unlimited (the default). --runtime-enabled, --no-runtime-enabled Autolaunch the model on the drone. Default enabled.

docs.title: Supported model types
docs.text:
Output format Model family yolov2_grid YOLOv2 / TinyYOLOv2 (grid + anchors) yolov5_flat YOLOv5 ONNX export yolov8_flat YOLOv8 / YOLO11 ONNX export yolov8_seg YOLOv8/v11 segmentation yolo_e2e End-to-end YOLO with NMS in the model (YOLO26) yolo_e2e_seg End-to-end YOLO segmentation ssd_multi SSD (multi-output, e.g. TensorFlow exports) detr DETR transformer detectors ostrack OSTrack single-object tracker mixformerv2 MixFormerV2 single-object tracker

The model must take float32 image input; models with a clearly unsupported structure (image classifiers, float16 inputs, non-image inputs) are rejected with an explanation.

docs.title: Deploying to the drone
docs.text:
The easiest way is to push the package directly: interactive runs offer it after the zip is written, and scripts pass --push (with --drone-ip if the drone is not at the default 192.168.1.101):

blueye bundle-model yolov8n.onnx --yes --push

If the drone cannot be reached, the command fails with a clear message — the zip is still written and can be pushed later with blueye models upload.

The same operations are available programmatically through the SDK:

import blueye.sdk

# An observer takes no control, but lets the SDK send the rescan the drone needs to pick
# up the change
drone = blueye.sdk.Drone(connect_as_observer=True)
model = drone.cv_models.upload("yolov8n_package.zip")
drone.cv_models.set_enabled(model.directory, True)
drone.disconnect()

Without the SDK installed, the drone's HTTP endpoint accepts the package zip as a multipart upload (field name file):

curl -F "file=@yolov8n_package.zip" http://192.168.1.101/api/cv-models/upload

or use the Blunux Web App — open http://192.168.1.101 in a browser and upload the zip from the Computer Vision tab.

docs.title: Managing models on the drone — blueye models
docs.text:
Installed models are managed with the blueye models command, or interactively by running it without an action on a terminal:

blueye models list
blueye models upload yolov8n_package.zip
blueye models enable yolov8n-coco
blueye models set-device yolov8n-coco tensorrt-dla0
blueye models set-hz yolov8n-coco 10
blueye models warmup yolov8n-coco      # pre-build the TensorRT engine
blueye models download yolov8n-coco -o ~/packages
blueye models delete yolov8n-coco --force

Model names are the directory slugs shown by blueye models list. The enabled state is the autolaunch configuration; the API does not expose a live "running" status.

Action Meaning list Table of installed models: name, directory, type, format, size, enabled, device, rate. enable NAME, disable NAME Turn autolaunch on or off. set-device NAME DEVICE Execution provider: cuda, tensorrt, tensorrt-dla0 or tensorrt-dla1. set-hz NAME HZ Maximum inference rate; one of 0, 5, 10, 15. 0 means unlimited, the same setting bundle-model --runtime-hz max writes into a package. warmup NAME Build the inference engine now so the first launch is instant. TensorRT builds take minutes; the command waits. delete NAME [--force] Remove the package. Asks for confirmation on a terminal; --force skips the question and is required when not interactive. upload PACKAGE Upload a package zip, as bundle-model --push does. download NAME [-o PATH] Save a package zip from the drone to a file or directory (default: current directory). rescan Ask the drone's vision pipeline to re-read the package directory.

list and download only talk to the drone's HTTP API. The commands that change a model (upload, delete, enable, disable, set-device, set-hz) and the interactive session connect to the drone as an observer, taking no control, because the drone only picks a change up after the rescan message that the command sends once the change is in. blueye models rescan sends that message on its own, for changes made some other way. A rescan restarts every running model.

docs.title: Downloading dive logs — blueye logs
docs.text:
The drone's binary dive logs (.bez) can be listed and downloaded from the terminal. The command connects to the drone as an observer — taking no control:

blueye logs list                       # table of logs on the drone
blueye logs download --latest 1        # newest finished log to the current directory
blueye logs download --latest 1 --mcap # ...and convert it for Foxglove
blueye logs download --latest 1 --dives-only  # newest dive, skipping power-on logs
blueye logs download BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00002 -o ~/dives
blueye logs download --all --since 2026-06-01 --dives-only
blueye logs convert mydive.bez         # convert an already-downloaded log (no drone)
blueye logs                            # interactive: pick logs to download
Action Meaning list Table of the logs on the drone: name, start time, max depth, size, dive flag. download [NAMES...] Download logs by name, or the --latest N newest, or --all. Exactly one of the three. -o/--output DIR sets the destination (default: current directory); --mcap also converts each log. convert FILES... Convert .bez files already on disk to .mcap. -o/--output DIR sets the destination (default: next to each input). Needs no drone.

list, download, and the interactive view accept --dives-only, --since YYYY-MM-DD, and --until YYYY-MM-DD to narrow the selection; the interactive view is a single scrollable table (type to filter, space to select, sorted newest first). The drone writes a new log from power-on to power-off, so one log is always open while you are connected. --latest skips it and says so; list and the interactive view mark it as open. Pass its name to download it anyway, knowing the file stops at the drone's last flush. --mcap converts each downloaded log to a Foxglove-ready .mcap next to the .bez — blueye logs convert does the same for files already on disk. Both need the cli extra. See visualizing dive logs with Foxglove. For working with logs from Python (streaming, filtering, plotting), see logs from the drone.

docs.title: Third-party tools — blueye tools
docs.text: The blueye command is built to grow: besides the built-in commands, anyone can drop single-file Python tools into a per-user directory. The CLI discovers them automatically, lists them in blueye --help, and runs them as blueye <tool-name> ... — no SDK changes needed.

docs.title: Writing a tool
docs.text:
A tool is a normal Python script carrying PEP 723 inline metadata, extended with a [tool.blueye] table. It can import blueye.sdk like any other script:

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["pandas"]
#
# [tool.blueye]
# name = "export-logs"
# description = "Export the dive log index to CSV"
# min-sdk-version = "2.7.0"
# ///
import sys

import pandas as pd

from blueye.sdk import Drone


def main() -> int:
    drone = Drone(connect_as_observer=True)
    rows = [
        {"name": log.name, "start": log.start_time, "max_depth": log.max_depth_magnitude}
        for log in drone.logs
    ]
    pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv(sys.stdout, index=False)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

The [tool.blueye] keys:

Key Required Meaning name yes The subcommand name (blueye export-logs). Lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens; must start with a letter; at most 32 characters. description yes One line shown in blueye --help and blueye tools list. min-sdk-version no Minimum blueye.sdk version; a mismatch prints a warning but never blocks.

Arguments after the tool name are passed to the script verbatim, and its exit code becomes the CLI's exit code. Invocation is strictly blueye <tool-name> args....

Dependencies. A tool always runs on the same Python interpreter as the blueye command, so blueye.sdk and everything installed next to it are importable without being listed. Packages the tool needs beyond that go in the PEP 723 dependencies list. When uv is installed, the CLI runs the tool as uv run --with <package> ... python <script>: uv puts the listed packages in a cached environment layered on top of the CLI's own, without installing anything into it. The first run of a tool downloads its packages, so do that before heading out on the drone's Wi-Fi; later runs come from uv's cache. A package the CLI's environment already satisfies is never downloaded. An SDK installed in the per-user package folder (pip install --user, the fallback on system Pythons that refuse writes to site-packages) is added to the tool's module search path after uv's packages, since uv's layered environment does not read that folder on its own. Without uv, the listed packages must already be installed next to the SDK (pip install pandas into the same environment). The tool's requires-python is not enforced; the interpreter is the CLI's. uv's own [tool.uv.sources] table in the script is not read either; dependencies come from the package index.

docs.title: Installing and managing tools
docs.text:
blueye tools validate my_script.py   # check the metadata before installing
blueye tools install my_script.py    # copy it into the tools directory
blueye tools install my_script.py --force   # replace an installed tool of the same name
blueye tools list                    # built-ins + installed tools
blueye tools uninstall export-logs
blueye tools dir                     # print the resolved tools directory

Discovery scans the tools directory on every invocation and parses only the metadata block — tool code is never executed during discovery or listing.

The directory is resolved from the BLUEYE_CLI_TOOLS_DIR environment variable when set, otherwise from the platform default:

Platform Default tools directory macOS ~/Library/Application Support/blueye/cli-tools Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/blueye/cli-tools (or ~/.local/share/blueye/cli-tools) Windows %APPDATA%\blueye\cli-tools

Name collisions always resolve in favor of built-in commands; blueye tools list shows shadowed or invalid tools with the reason.

SDK contributors adding a built-in command should follow the recipe and invariants documented in the blueye.sdk.cli.commands module docstring.

docs.title: Configure drone parameters
docs.text: There are settings on the drone that are remotely configurable from the Blueye mobile app. These can also be set directly from the SDK.

docs.title: Configure time and date
docs.text:
The drone does not keep track of time internally. When a client connects and is in control, the SDK sends the computer's current time to the drone. A connection made with connect_as_observer=True, or while another client holds control, leaves the drone's clock alone, unless it passes disconnect_other_clients=True and takes control. You can also set the time yourself:

import time
from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()

myDrone.config.set_drone_time(int(time.time()))  # Unix timestamp

The drone's clock runs in UTC and stamps its logs, so always set it to the current Unix time. To show local time in the video overlay, set the overlay's time zone offset in minutes instead. The overlay adds it to the drone's UTC time:

myDrone.camera.overlay.set_timezone_offset(120)  # UTC+2

docs.title: Calibrate pressure sensor for water density
docs.text:
The water density on the drone default to a reasonable density for salt water: 1025 grams per liter. For more accurate depth readings, the water density can be configured manually to suit your local conditions

from blueye.sdk import Drone, WaterDensities

myDrone = Drone()

# Salt water
myDrone.config.set_water_density(WaterDensities.salty)  # 1025 g/L

# Brackish water
myDrone.config.set_water_density(WaterDensities.brackish)  # 1011 g/L

# Fresh water
myDrone.config.set_water_density(WaterDensities.fresh)  # 997 g/L

# Can also be set to arbitrary values
myDrone.config.set_water_density(1234)

docs.title: Configure camera parameters
docs.text:
There are several camera parameters that can be set. For a full list of camera parameters and their possible values see the camera reference section.

To change a single parameter you can set it directly:

from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()

myDrone.camera.set_bitrate(8_000_000)  # 8 Mbit bitrate

To change multiple parameters at once, use the configure() context manager. This batches all changes into a single request, avoiding multiple pipeline restarts:

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()

with myDrone.camera.configure(timeout=5.0) as params:
    params.stream_resolution = bp.Resolution.RESOLUTION_FULLHD_1080P
    params.framerate = 30
    params.bitrate = 4_000_000
# All changes are sent in one request when the block exits.
# If an exception occurs inside the block, changes are discarded.

The timeout parameter (default: 0.5s) controls how long to wait for the drone to respond. Increase it when changing parameters that trigger pipeline restarts (e.g. codec, resolution).

Setters send every parameter

Each camera setter sends the full set of camera parameters, not only the one it changes. It fills in the rest from the parameters the SDK read last: on the first setter call, or by the most recent getter. A change made from the Blueye app after that read is written back over, and two setters in a row can undo each other if a getter ran in between. configure() reads the parameters when the block starts and sends one request, so use it when changing several parameters. The overlay setters work the same way with the overlay parameters. Sending only the changed field is tracked in #221.

Exposure and white balance apply to every model, with -1 for automatic: set_exposure and set_whitebalance. set_gain differs per model: -1 keeps the current gain on the Pioneer, Pro, X1 and X3, and on the X3 Ultra and X7 a manual gain only takes effect with a manual exposure. set_hue only has an effect on the Pioneer, Pro, X1 and X3.

docs.title: Image settings (X3 Ultra and X7)
docs.text:
The 4K camera in the X3 Ultra and X7 has image settings the older cameras lack. The setters need Blunux 5.0.0 and raise RuntimeError on older versions. They do not check the model.

Setter Range Default set_brightness -10..10 0 set_contrast -50..50 0 set_saturation 0..50 8 set_gamma 4..79 22 set_sharpness -20..20 -20 set_backlight_compensation -150..150 10 set_denoise -20..20 -20 enable_ehdr True or False True set_ehdr_exposure_min_number 1..4 1 set_ehdr_exposure_max_number 1..4 2

More than 2 eHDR frames can lower the frame rate.

with myDrone.camera.configure() as params:
    params.contrast = 10
    params.saturation = 12
    params.denoise = 0

docs.title: Image filters and digital pan, tilt and zoom
docs.text:
The 4K camera in the X3 Ultra and X7 has two image filters and a digital pan, tilt and zoom. They are not camera parameters, each is sent as its own control message, and the drone reports the state it applied in a telemetry message. The setters raise RuntimeError on other models, on the guestport camera and on drones running Blunux older than 5.0.0.

from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()

# Turbidity filter: contrast enhancement (CLAHE) for murky water
myDrone.camera.set_turbidity_filter(enabled=True, intensity=0.5)

# Color correction: restores the red and blue the water absorbs with depth
myDrone.camera.set_color_correction(enabled=True, intensity=0.8)

# Digital pan, tilt and zoom. Values left out keep what was last sent from this object, so
# the second call keeps the zoom of the first.
myDrone.camera.set_pan_tilt_zoom(zoom=0.5)
myDrone.camera.set_pan_tilt_zoom(pan=-0.3, tilt=0.2)

print(myDrone.camera.get_turbidity_filter())  # FilterMessage with enabled and intensity
print(myDrone.camera.get_pan_tilt_zoom())  # CameraPanTiltZoom with pan, tilt and zoom

The drone publishes TurbidityFilterTel, ColorCorrectionTel and CameraPanTiltZoomTel when the state changes, not at a fixed rate. The getters return what the drone reported on the last change, and ask the drone directly if nothing has been received since connecting, so there is no need to wait for a periodic update. A drone that has never applied a filter has nothing to report, and the getter returns None until the first change.

The report arrives about 0.1 s after the command, so set_pan_tilt_zoom fills in the values you leave out from what it last sent, and from the drone's report only before the first call. A change made by the Blueye app after your last call is not picked up that way; pass all three values when that matters.

Laser dot tracking works on the full, unzoomed image, so enable_tracking resets pan, tilt and zoom to 0 when it starts, as the Blueye app does.

docs.title: Recording and streaming
docs.text:
The settings for the recorded file, its resolution, codec and bitrate, are covered in Recording video and taking pictures. The live stream has these:

  • set_stream_resolution and set_framerate. The frame rate applies to the recording too.
  • set_bitrate: the H.264 stream bitrate, 1 to 16 Mbit/s.
  • set_streaming_protocol: STREAMING_PROTOCOL_RTSP_H264 or STREAMING_PROTOCOL_RTSP_MJPEG. The Pioneer, Pro, X1 and X3 do not start a recording while they stream MJPEG. The X3 Ultra and X7 cap an MJPEG stream at 1080p.
  • set_mtu_size: the largest network packet the stream uses, in bytes. 0 uses the drone's default of 1400. Lower it for links that carry smaller packets, such as some VPNs. Needs Blunux 5.1.0.
import blueye.protocol as bp

with myDrone.camera.configure(timeout=5.0) as params:
    params.streaming_protocol = bp.StreamingProtocol.STREAMING_PROTOCOL_RTSP_H264
    params.mtu_size = 1200

docs.title: Camera tilt
docs.text:
Every model except the original Pioneer can tilt the camera. Drone.features contains "tilt" on those drones, and the Tilt methods raise RuntimeError without it.

import time

myDrone.camera.tilt.set_velocity(0.5)  # 1 is full speed up, -1 full speed down
time.sleep(1)
myDrone.camera.tilt.set_velocity(0)
print(myDrone.camera.tilt.get_angle())  # Degrees

myDrone.camera.tilt.enable_stabilization(True)

The drone keeps the last velocity until it gets a new one, so the tilt runs to its end stop unless you set it back to 0. Stabilization tilts the camera against the drone's pitch. The X7 accepts the setting but its tilt servo does not compensate.

docs.title: Overlay and logo
docs.text:
The overlay is the text and logo the drone draws into its recordings. camera.overlay has an enable_* method for each field (depth, heading, tilt, date, temperature, altitude, distance and more), and setters for the title and subtitle, units, font size, margins, text shading, the date format and the time zone offset.

import blueye.protocol as bp

overlay = myDrone.camera.overlay
overlay.enable_depth(True)
overlay.enable_date(True)
overlay.set_date_format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
overlay.set_title("Pier inspection")
overlay.set_depth_unit(bp.DepthUnit.DEPTH_UNIT_METERS)
overlay.set_font_size(bp.FontSize.FONT_SIZE_PX25)

Title, subtitle and date format take up to 63 ASCII characters. Longer text is cut to 63 characters and sent with a RuntimeWarning. Non-ASCII text, a value of the wrong type or one out of range is not sent: the setter warns with a RuntimeWarning and leaves the setting unchanged.

To show your own logo, upload a JPG or PNG of up to 2000 px and 5 MB, then select it:

overlay.upload_logo("logo.png")
overlay.set_logo(bp.LogoType.LOGO_TYPE_CUSTOM)

LOGO_TYPE_DEFAULT shows the default logo and LOGO_TYPE_NONE none. download_logo fetches the uploaded file and delete_logo removes it.

docs.title: Connecting to the drone
docs.text: A Drone object connects when it is created and stays connected until you call disconnect or the script exits. This page covers what the drone does while a client is connected, when that client goes quiet, and when it leaves.

docs.title: Choosing how to connect
docs.text:
Connections require Blunux 3.2 or newer. Use an observer connection for telemetry, log downloads, or other work that should leave control with the pilot:

import time
from blueye.sdk import Drone

with Drone(connect_as_observer=True, log_notifications=True) as drone:
    time.sleep(1)  # Allow the first telemetry messages to arrive.
    print(drone.get_depth())  # Can still be None if no depth message has arrived.

The default Drone() connection is eligible for control. If nobody holds control, it takes control, zeroes the thruster setpoints and synchronizes the drone's clock to the computer. If another client already holds control, it joins without displacing that client, but can inherit control when that client leaves.

Argument Effect ip="192.168.1.101" Drone address; change it for a routed network. connect_as_observer=True Exclude this connection from control assignment and handover. disconnect_other_clients=True Disconnect clients holding control until this non-observer connection has control. Ignored for an observer connection. log_notifications=True Log incoming drone notifications through Python's logging module. Configure logging to display them. client_info=... Supply a blueye.protocol.ClientInfo; otherwise the SDK identifies itself using its version, OS and hostname. auto_connect=False Construct the object without connecting; call connect() later.

connect_as_observer, notification logging and the other connection options must be passed to connect() itself when using auto_connect=False; they are not saved for a later call.

docs.title: Using the Blueye app alongside a script
docs.text:
The Blueye app initially joins as an observer. When the pilot starts a dive, it requests control if nobody has it; otherwise it reports the client in control and refuses to start the dive. A plain Drone() script can therefore block the pilot even if the app connected first. Use connect_as_observer=True for read-only scripts.

An observer connection is not a read-only permission: setters still send commands. The depth callback example deliberately changes a shared telemetry rate to demonstrate the API; omit those changes when another client's rate must be preserved. See telemetry subscriptions.

docs.title: Inspecting clients and taking control
docs.text:
get_connected_clients and get_client_in_control read the latest client-list telemetry. Both return None until it arrives. Once available, client id 0 means nobody holds control.

with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) as drone:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 5
    clients = drone.get_connected_clients()
    while clients is None and time.monotonic() < deadline:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        clients = drone.get_connected_clients()
    for client in clients or []:
        print(client.client_id, client.client_info.name, client.client_info.is_observer)
    print("Client in control:", drone.get_client_in_control())

take_control() disconnects other clients until this client is in control; it is not a cooperative handover request. Coordinate with the pilot before calling it or connecting with disconnect_other_clients=True. An observer is excluded from promotion, so take_control() cannot turn an observer into a controller and may disconnect other clients before timing out. Disconnect and reconnect as a non-observer if control is needed.

docs.title: The watchdog
docs.text:
The drone expects a watchdog message from every connected client. The SDK sends one every second from a background thread for as long as the connection is open. The drone keeps two timers on these messages: a 3 second safety timer for the client in control, described below, and a client list that drops a client after about 4 seconds of silence.

The thread is a daemon thread, so it stops when the Python interpreter exits. A script that ends right after starting something on the drone, a mission for example, has stopped petting the watchdog 3 seconds before the drone notices.

docs.title: What the drone does when the client in control goes quiet
docs.text:
Only watchdog messages from the client in control count for the drone's safety timer. When they stop for 3 seconds, the drone runs its failsafe once:

  • All auto modes are switched off: auto depth, auto heading, auto altitude, station keeping, weather vaning and the mission autopilot.
  • The stick input is zeroed, boost and slow included.
  • The main lights and a guest-port light are switched off.
  • The laser is switched off and laser dot tracking stops.
  • The multibeam stops.
  • The gripper stops moving.
  • Running computer vision models are stopped.
  • A running mission is aborted and its state becomes MISSION_STATE_ABORTED.

The failsafe also runs 3 seconds after the client in control disconnects, unless another client has taken over control by then.

docs.title: Control handover
docs.text:
The first client to connect without connect_as_observer=True is in control. When the client in control disconnects, or is dropped from the client list after about 4 seconds of silence, the drone hands control to the client that has been connected the longest among those that did not connect as observers. If there is none, nobody is in control and the drone reports client id 0.

Drone.in_control is set when the connection is made and by take_control. It is not updated afterwards, so after a handover it is stale. Compare get_client_in_control with client_id for the current answer:

from blueye.sdk import Drone

d = Drone()
in_control_now = d.get_client_in_control() == d.client_id

docs.title: Observers
docs.text: Drone(connect_as_observer=True) keeps a client out of the handover: it is never given control. It does not make the SDK read-only. Every setter still sends its message, and the drone acts on control messages from any client. An observer's watchdog messages do not count for the safety timer either, so an observer cannot keep the failsafe from running when the client in control goes away.

docs.title: Ending the connection
docs.text: Call disconnect when the script is done. The drone removes the client at once and hands control over without waiting for the 3 second timeout. Scripts that start a mission should stay connected until the mission has ended, see Mission planning.

docs.title: Deprecated properties
docs.text:
v2.8.0 replaced the properties that exposed drone state and control with explicit getter and setter methods. The old names still work but emit a DeprecationWarning on every read and write, and they will be removed in v3. Code written for v2.0 to v2.7 can be updated one name at a time with the tables below.

The warning names the replacement. Python shows each deprecation warning once per location by default; to see every use a script makes while it runs, turn them all on:

python -W always::DeprecationWarning my_script.py

Motion.current_thruster_setpoints is read-only, like the other properties without a setter below. Set the setpoints with send_thruster_setpoint() or the individual setters. Assigning to a read-only property raises AttributeError.

Camera.resolution maps to get_resolution() and set_resolution(), which are deprecated as well, and drones running Blunux 4.4 or newer ignore that resolution. Use set_stream_resolution() and set_recording_resolution() instead, and their getters to read the values back.

The tables are generated from the list the test suite checks, so every row has a test behind it.

docs.title: Drone model and hardware
docs.text:
The drone publishes its identity and hardware configuration in the DroneInfoTel telemetry message. The Drone class exposes the most useful fields through getters, so a script can adapt to the drone it is connected to without parsing the message itself. The getters return None until the first DroneInfoTel message has been received, which normally happens during connect.

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone

drone = Drone()

# The model as a blueye.protocol.Model enum, e.g. bp.Model.MODEL_X7
model = drone.get_model()

# True for the X3 Ultra and X7, which have the 4K camera
if drone.is_jetson_platform():
    drone.camera.set_framerate(60)

# bp.PowerSource.POWER_SOURCE_PARALLEL_BATTERIES on the X7, SINGLE_BATTERY on the others
power_source = drone.get_power_source()

# E.g. bp.PressureSensorType.PRESSURE_SENSOR_TYPE_KELLER_PA7LD for the extended depth sensor
depth_sensor = drone.get_depth_sensor_type()

The full DroneInfo message is available through get_drone_info. It also carries the component serial numbers, the guest port configuration and the installed computer vision models.

drone_info = drone.get_drone_info()
print(drone_info.blunux_version)
print(drone_info.serial_number.decode())

The main camera calibration published by the X3 Ultra and X7 is covered in Camera calibration.

docs.title: Visualize live sensor data from the drone with Foxglove
docs.text:
With some simple steps you can visualize live sensor data from the drone in Foxglove.

  1. Download foxglove here and create an account.
  2. Power on the drone and connect your computer to the Blueye wifi.
  3. Run pip install "blueye.sdk[examples]" to get the necessary dependencies, if you have not done so already.
  4. Clone the blueye.sdk repository to get the examples, or copy the script below into a file. In the examples folder you simply run python foxglove_bridge_ws.py to start the bridge.
  5. Open foxglove and open a new Foxglove WebSocket connection and leave it on default (ws://localhost:8765).
  6. Add panel, Raw message, or Plot and select the topic you want to display.

docs.title: Alternative with Docker
docs.text:
We have also provided a docker container that you can use to automatically starts the blueye-foxglove server.

  1. Pull the image: docker pull blueyerobotics/foxglove-bridge.
  2. Run the image in a container with port 8765 open: docker run --rm -p 8765:8765 blueyerobotics/foxglove-bridge.
  3. Connect as above in step 5.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The script below uses the Blueye SDK to subscribe to the drone telemetry messages with ZeroMQ. Then the foxglove websocket server is forwarding the protobuf messages so they can be subscribed to in the Foxglove GUI.

docs.title: Visualize entire dive logs
docs.text: With our .bez to .mcap log file converter you can easily visualize all the logged data from a dive. Check out the Logfile to MCAP converter to get started.

docs.title: Example of a websocket bridge
docs.text:
examples/foxglove_bridge_ws.py 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import time
import logging

from blueye.sdk import Drone

import asyncio
import time
import base64
from foxglove_websocket import run_cancellable
from foxglove_websocket.server import FoxgloveServer
import sys
import inspect
from google.protobuf import descriptor_pb2
import blueye.protocol

# Declare the global variable
channel_ids = {}
global_server = None

logger = logging.getLogger("FoxgloveBridge")
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s: [%(levelname)s] <%(name)s> %(message)s"))
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.info("Starting Foxglove bridge")

logger_sdk = logging.getLogger(blueye.sdk.__name__)
logger_sdk.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
logger_sdk.addHandler(handler)


def parse_message(payload_msg_name, data):
    global global_server
    global channel_ids

    if payload_msg_name in channel_ids:
        try:
            asyncio.run(
                global_server.send_message(channel_ids[payload_msg_name], time.time_ns(), data)
            )
        except TypeError as e:
            logger.info(f"Error sending message for {payload_msg_name}: {e}")
    else:
        logger.info(f"Warning: Channel ID not found for message type: {payload_msg_name}")


def add_file_descriptor_and_dependencies(file_descriptor, file_descriptor_set):
    """Recursively add descriptors and their dependencies to the FileDescriptorSet"""
    # Check if the descriptor is already in the FileDescriptorSet
    if file_descriptor.name not in [fd.name for fd in file_descriptor_set.file]:
        # Add the descriptor to the FileDescriptorSet
        file_descriptor.CopyToProto(file_descriptor_set.file.add())

        # Recursively add dependencies
        for file_descriptor_dep in file_descriptor.dependencies:
            add_file_descriptor_and_dependencies(file_descriptor_dep, file_descriptor_set)


def get_protobuf_descriptors(namespace):
    descriptors = {}

    # Get the module corresponding to the namespace
    module = sys.modules[namespace]

    # Iterate through all the attributes of the module
    for name, obj in inspect.getmembers(module):
        # Check if the object is a class, ends with 'Tel', and has a _meta attribute with pb
        if (
            inspect.isclass(obj)
            and name.endswith("Tel")
            and hasattr(obj, "_meta")
            and hasattr(obj._meta, "pb")
        ):
            try:
                # Access the DESCRIPTOR
                descriptor = obj._meta.pb.DESCRIPTOR

                # Create a FileDescriptorSet
                file_descriptor_set = descriptor_pb2.FileDescriptorSet()

                # Add the descriptor and its dependencies
                add_file_descriptor_and_dependencies(descriptor.file, file_descriptor_set)

                # Serialize the FileDescriptorSet to binary
                serialized_data = file_descriptor_set.SerializeToString()

                # Base64 encode the serialized data
                schema_base64 = base64.b64encode(serialized_data).decode("utf-8")

                # Store the serialized data in the dictionary
                descriptors[name] = schema_base64
            except AttributeError as e:
                logger.info(f"Skipping message: {name}: {e}")
                # Skip non-message types
                raise e

    return descriptors


async def main():
    # Initialize the drone
    myDrone = Drone(connect_as_observer=True)
    myDrone.telemetry.add_msg_callback([], parse_message, raw=True)

    # Specify the server's host, port, and a human-readable name
    async with FoxgloveServer("0.0.0.0", 8765, "Blueye SDK bridge") as server:
        global global_server
        global_server = server

        # Get Protobuf descriptors for all relevant message types
        namespace = "blueye.protocol"
        descriptors = get_protobuf_descriptors(namespace)

        # Register each message type as a channel
        for message_name, schema_base64 in descriptors.items():
            chan_id = await global_server.add_channel(
                {
                    "topic": message_name,  # Using the message name as the topic
                    "encoding": "protobuf",
                    "schemaName": f"blueye.protocol.{message_name}",
                    "schema": schema_base64,
                }
            )
            # Store the chan_id in the map
            channel_ids[message_name] = chan_id

        for name, chan_id in channel_ids.items():
            logger.info(f"Registered topic: blueye.protocol.{name}")

        # Keep the server running
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.text:
GET /srt

Downloads a subtitle file (srt) for a video file containing log data from the dive. The data is gathered from the videos accompanying logfile. By passing in varius queries it is possible to select which data one wants displayed, and where to display it.

Input parameters

Parameter In Type Default Minimum Maximum Nullable Description date-format query string %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S No Format of the date/time. field-date query integer 0 No Enable or disable the date field. "1" to enable, "0" to disable. field-depth query integer 1 No Enable or disable the depth field. "1" to enable, "0" to disable. field-heading query integer 1 No Enable or disable the heading field. "1" to enable, "0" to disable. field-temp query integer 1 No Enable or disable the temperature field. "1" to enable, "0" to disable. field-tilt query integer 0 No Enable or disable the tilt field. "1" to enable, "0" to disable. fileRequired query string No Name of the videofile to download subtitle file for. format query string srt No Subtitles can also be retrived in the WEBVTT format. Use format=vtt toget a .vtt file instead of a .srt file. length-units query string meter No Unit to use for length. Use "meter" for metric units, and "feet" forimperial. placement query string top No Where to place the subtitle. Use "top" for placing on the top, "bottom"for placing on the bottom, and "" for using the player default. temp-units query string celsius No Unit to use for temperature. Use "celsius" for metric units, and"fahrenheit" for imperial. title query string No Title of the video. tz-offset query integer 0 No The drone stores all time in UTC+0, so if you were diving in anothertimezone and want to correct for that in the displayed time you can add a timezone offset here. Theunit is minutes and both positive and negative values are supported. Response 200 OK text/srt

Subtitle file for the requested video file

Schema 
{
    "type": "object",
    "description": "Subtitle file for the requested video file"
}
Response 400 Bad Request text/plain

No video file given or other bad request

Schema 
{
    "description": "No video file given or other bad request"
}
Response 404 Not Found text/plain

Log file not found or invalid format/placement

Schema 
{
    "description": "Log file not found or invalid format/placement"
}

docs.title: Upgrading to v2
docs.text:
Version 2 of the Blueye SDK introduces a few breaking changes. The following guide outlines what has changed, and what you need to change to be compatible with the new version.

The examples below use the getter and setter methods introduced in v2.8.0. The v2.0 to v2.7 property names still work but emit a DeprecationWarning; the deprecated properties page maps each of them to its replacement.

docs.title: Change of underlying communication protocol
docs.text:
The underlying communications protocol has been changed from UDP/TCP to protobuf messages sent over ZeroMQ sockets. This means that the drone now supports multiple simultaneous clients, and as such, the 'slave-mode' functionality is no longer necessary and has been removed.

Another added benefit is the ability to list and disconnect other clients connected to the drone.

docs.title: Requirement on Blunux v3.2 or newer
docs.text: The SDK now requires v3.2 or newer of the Blunux operating system to be installed on the drone to able to connect to it.

docs.title: Dropped support Python 3.7
docs.text: One or several of our subdependencies has dropped support for 3.7, and in an effort to reduce the maintenance burden we decided to drop support for 3.7 when adding support for 3.11.

docs.title: New range for lights control
docs.text:
Previously the valid range for the lights was an int between 0 and 255, it has now been updated to a float in the range 0 to 1.

# Previously
my_drone.lights = 64

# Updated
my_drone.set_lights(0.25)

docs.title: Error flags are a dictionary of bools
docs.text:
Error flags are now represented as a dictionary of bools instead of bitflags in an int. See the ErrorFlags message for an overview of the possible error states.

# Previously
depth_read_error: bool = my_drone.error_flags & (1 << 2)

# Updated
depth_read_error: bool = my_drone.get_error_flags()["depth_read"]

docs.title: Changed return type for the active video streams
docs.text:
The active video streams are returned as a dictionary containing "main" and "guestport" as keys. This change provides the option to be able to read the number of active video streams for both the main camera and (optionally) a guestport camera. 

# Previously
streams_on_main_camera = my_drone.active_video_streams

# Updated
streams_on_main_camera = my_drone.get_active_video_streams()["main"]

docs.title: Water density is still in g/L
docs.text:
An earlier version of this guide said that the water density unit changed from grams per liter to kilograms per liter. It did not. The SDK, the protocol and the drone all use grams per liter, and salt water is 1025, which is also WaterDensities.salty. Code that followed the old advice and sent 1.025 gave the drone a density a thousand times too low for its depth calculation.

from blueye.sdk.constants import WaterDensities

my_drone.config.set_water_density(WaterDensities.salty)  # 1025 g/L

docs.title: Camera Stabilization uses on/off instead of toggle
docs.text:
The camera stabilization functionality now uses separate methods for enabling and disabling instead of a single toggle method. The methods live on camera.tilt.

# Previously
my_drone.camera.toggle_stabilization()
print(my_drone.camera.stabilization_enabled)

# Updated
my_drone.camera.tilt.enable_stabilization(True)
print(my_drone.camera.tilt.is_stabilization_enabled())

docs.title: tilt_speed has been renamed to tilt_velocity
docs.text:
The function tilt_speed has been renamed to tilt_velocity to better reflect its purpose and usage. Update your code to use the new function name. 

# Previously
my_drone.camera.tilt.set_speed(1)

# Updated
my_drone.camera.tilt.set_velocity(1)

docs.title: New subclass for battery data
docs.text:
The battery state of charge has been moved to a subclass on the Drone-object. In addition the state of charge range for the battery has been adjusted to a scale of 0 to 1, instead of the previous 0 to 100 range.

# Previously
state_of_charge: int = my_drone.battery_state_of_charge

# Updated
state_of_charge: float = my_drone.battery.get_state_of_charge()

docs.title: Custom Overlay Classes Replaced with Enums
docs.text:
Custom overlay classes have been replaced with enums defined in the blueye.protocol package. Make sure to update your code to use the new enums for overlay functionality.

# Previously
from blueye.sdk import DepthUnitOverlay, FontSizeOverlay, LogoOverlay, TemperatureUnitOverlay

my_drone.camera.overlay.depth_unit = DepthUnitOverlay.METERS
my_drone.camera.overlay.font_size = FontSizeOverlay.PX15
my_drone.camera.overlay.logo = LogoOverlay.BLUEYE
my_drone.camera.overlay.temperature_unit = TemperatureUnitOverlay.CELSIUS

# Updated
import blueye.protocol as bp

my_drone.camera.overlay.set_depth_unit(bp.DepthUnit.DEPTH_UNIT_METERS)
my_drone.camera.overlay.set_font_size(bp.FontSize.FONT_SIZE_PX15)
my_drone.camera.overlay.set_logo(bp.LogoType.LOGO_TYPE_DEFAULT)
my_drone.camera.overlay.set_temperature_unit(bp.TemperatureUnit.TEMPERATURE_UNIT_CELSIUS)

docs.title: Telemetry getters return None if no data exists
docs.text:
Getters that read telemetry data, such as get_lights, camera.tilt.get_angle, get_depth, get_pose, battery.get_state_of_charge, get_error_flags, get_active_video_streams, motion.is_auto_depth_active, and motion.is_auto_heading_active, return None if no telemetry message has been received from the drone. Previously if a UDP message had not arrived, a KeyError exception would have been raised.

# Previously
print(my_drone.pose) # If no state message has been received yet this could throw a KeyError

# Updated
print(my_drone.get_pose()) # This will now print "None" if no AttitudeTel-message has been received.

docs.title: New initialization parameters to the Drone object
docs.text:
The AutoConnect parameter has been renamed to auto_connect for consistency and clarity. 

# Previously
my_drone = Drone(AutoConnect = False)

# Updated
my_drone = Drone(auto_connect = False)

The udpTimeout parameter has been renamed to timeout for consistency and clarity. 

# Previously
my_drone = Drone(udpTimeout = 5)

# Updated
my_drone = Drone(timeout = 5)

docs.title: Mission planning with the SDK
docs.text: The SDK supports creating and running missions on the drone using the mission attribute of the Drone class. Missions are created using a set of instructions that define the actions the drone should perform.

docs.title: Creating a mission
docs.text:
As an example we will create a mission that goes to the seabed, takes a picture with the main camera, and returns to the surface.

First we define the instructions we want to use. The available instructions are outlined in the Instruction class.

import blueye.protocol as bp

go_to_seabed = bp.Instruction(go_to_seabed_command={"desired_speed": 0.3})
take_picture = bp.Instruction(camera_command={
    "camera_action": bp.CameraAction.CAMERA_ACTION_TAKE_PHOTO
})
go_to_surface = bp.Instruction(go_to_surface_command={"desired_speed": 0.3})

Next we create the mission using these instructions. The mission is created by passing a list of instructions to the prepare_new_mission function. It copies the instructions and numbers them 1 to n in list order, the same numbering the Blueye app uses. The drone reports progress by these ids in MissionStatus.completed_instruction_ids and ReferenceAutoPilot.active_instruction_id.

from blueye.sdk.mission import prepare_new_mission
go_to_seabed_mission = prepare_new_mission(
    instruction_list = [go_to_seabed, take_picture, go_to_surface],
    mission_id = 0,
    mission_name = "Go to seabed and take a picture",
)

docs.title: Loading and running the mission
docs.text:
With the mission created we can now transfer it to the drone and run it. The easiest way to do this is to use the load_and_run method, which will transfer the mission the drone, wait for it to become ready and then start the mission.

load_and_run returns as soon as the drone has been told to start. Keep the script connected until the mission has ended: the SDK pets the drone's watchdog from a background thread, and when the script exits the drone aborts the mission about 3 seconds later. See Connecting to the drone for what else the drone does then.

A mission does not always end in MISSION_STATE_COMPLETED. The drone aborts it (MISSION_STATE_ABORTED) when it loses its position for more than 3 seconds, when it is stuck, when a waypoint is too far away, or when the watchdog fires. A mission with waypoints that is started without a valid position ends in MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_START_MISSION. Another client can clear the mission, which shows as MISSION_STATE_INACTIVE, or load its own in place of yours, which passes through MISSION_STATE_INACTIVE to MISSION_STATE_READY or MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_LOAD_MISSION. A restart of the drone's mission node also reports MISSION_STATE_INACTIVE. Wait for all of these, and treat a status of None as not reported yet. load_and_run returns after the drone has reported MISSION_STATE_READY for the new mission, so an INACTIVE read afterwards is not left over from before it. A replacement loaded within the same second can show MISSION_STATE_READY without an INACTIVE in between, which the loop below does not catch; a script that must detect that can give its mission a nonzero mission_id and compare it with MissionStatus.id, which the drone reports for the mission it holds.

import time

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone

d = Drone()

d.mission.load_and_run(go_to_seabed_mission)

end_states = (
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_COMPLETED,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_ABORTED,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_START_MISSION,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_LOAD_MISSION,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_INACTIVE,
)
status = d.mission.get_status()
while status is None or status.state not in end_states:
    time.sleep(0.1)
    status = d.mission.get_status()
print(f"Mission ended with state {status.state.name}")

d.disconnect()

docs.title: Sensor requirements
docs.text:
Some instructions need a sensor the drone may not have. The drone checks them when the mission starts and while it runs:

Instruction Needs Without it Waypoint, go to home A valid position estimate. A DVL, the drone's own Blueye GNSS, UGPS, USBL or NMEA input over UDP all count, unlike for station keeping. The mission does not start: MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_START_MISSION with a NOTIFICATION_TYPE_DRONE_POSITION_IS_UNKNOWN notification. A running mission is aborted after 3 seconds without a valid position. Go to home The pilot's position as well, sent to the drone as PilotGPSPositionCtrl. The Blueye app sends it; the SDK has no method for it yet. The drone reports the position it holds in PilotGPSPositionTel. The drone reports NOTIFICATION_TYPE_USER_POSITION_IS_UNKNOWN and does not move on from the instruction. Pause or clear the mission. Photos by distance (CAMERA_ACTION_TAKE_PHOTOS_DISTANCE) A valid position estimate, as for waypoints. The drone reports NOTIFICATION_TYPE_DRONE_POSITION_IS_UNKNOWN and takes no photos. Depth set point measured from the seabed An altitude sensor: a DVL or a downward-facing Ping sonar. Without any altitude report the instruction is skipped with NOTIFICATION_TYPE_INSTRUCTION_SKIPPED. With a sensor that has no valid reading yet, the drone descends as if the bottom were 50 m below until the sensor sees it. Tilt multibeam servo A multibeam servo on a guest port. The instruction is skipped with NOTIFICATION_TYPE_INSTRUCTION_SKIPPED. Go to seabed, go to surface, depth set point from the surface, single photo, photos by time, tilt, wait Nothing beyond the built-in sensors.

The drone also aborts a mission when a waypoint is more than 300 m away, when it detects that it is stuck (NOTIFICATION_TYPE_DRONE_IS_STUCK), and when the client in control stops petting the watchdog, see Connecting to the drone. PositionEstimateTel.position_estimate.is_valid is the position validity the mission checks, navigation_sensors in the same message lists each sensor with its own validity, and get_altitude returns None while the altitude is not valid.

docs.title: Getting status updates from the mission
docs.text:
The mission progress is published through the NotificationTel messages. These messages can be read manually with the usual telemetry methods, ie. telemetry.get or telemetry.add_msg_callback.

Alternatively, if one initializes the Drone object with log_notifications=True, the notifications will be logged with pythons logging module. This is the recommended way to get notified about mission progress.

from blueye.sdk import Drone

d = Drone(log_notifications=True)

The termial output can however quickly become cluttered when the logs are being printed inbetween the program output. In such cases, it can be useful to run the program in one terminal and then run a separate terminal to read the logs. This can be accomplished by configuring a simple TCP server to listen for log messages. See the Receiving logs in another terminal section for an example of how to do this.

docs.title: Exporting to JSON
docs.text:
The mission can be exported to a JSON file using the export_to_json method. This allows you to save the mission for later use or share it with others. It is also possible to load the json file in the Blueye App.

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk.mission import export_to_json, prepare_new_mission

# Create a mission
mission = prepare_new_mission(
    instruction_list=[bp.Instruction(go_to_seabed_command={"desired_speed": 0.3})]
)

# Export the mission to a JSON file
export_to_json(mission, "exported_mission.json")

docs.title: Importing from JSON
docs.text:
You can also import a mission from a JSON file using the import_from_json method. This allows you to load a previously saved mission and run it on the drone.

from blueye.sdk import Drone
from blueye.sdk.mission import import_from_json

mission = import_from_json("exported_mission.json")

d = Drone()
d.mission.load_and_run(mission)
# Stay connected until the mission has ended, as shown above

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Here are some examples outlining how to use some of the mission planning features

Tilt camera

This is a simple example that tilts the camera up and down. Useful for testing with the drone out of the water. The drone limits a tilt instruction to its own tilt range: ±30° on the Pro, X1, X3 and X3 Ultra and ±90° on the X7, see Blueye drone models.

examples/mission_tilt.py 

import logging
import logging.handlers
import time

import blueye.protocol as bp

from blueye.sdk import Drone
from blueye.sdk.mission import prepare_new_mission

# Publish runtime logs over TCP (including mission status notifications)
logger = logging.getLogger("blueye.sdk")
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
socket_handler = logging.handlers.SocketHandler(
    "localhost", logging.handlers.DEFAULT_TCP_LOGGING_PORT
)
logger.addHandler(socket_handler)

# Create some instructions for the mission
tilt_camera_center = bp.Instruction(tilt_main_camera_command={"tilt_angle": {"value": 0.0}})
tilt_camera_top = bp.Instruction(tilt_main_camera_command={"tilt_angle": {"value": 30.0}})
tilt_camera_bottom = bp.Instruction(tilt_main_camera_command={"tilt_angle": {"value": -30.0}})
wait = bp.Instruction(wait_for_command={"wait_for_seconds": 4})

# Create a mission with the instructions
mission = prepare_new_mission(
    instruction_list=[tilt_camera_top, wait, tilt_camera_bottom, wait, tilt_camera_center, wait],
    mission_id=0,
    mission_name="Tilt camera",
)

# Establish a connection to the drone
d = Drone(log_notifications=True)

# Send the mission to the drone and start it
d.mission.load_and_run(mission)

# Stay connected until the mission has ended. If the script exits, the SDK stops petting the
# drone's watchdog and the drone aborts the mission about 3 seconds later. The status is None
# until the drone has reported one, and a mission can end aborted or failed as well as completed.
# It is also over when another client clears it (INACTIVE) or loads its own in its place
# (INACTIVE, then READY or FAILED_TO_LOAD_MISSION).
end_states = (
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_COMPLETED,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_ABORTED,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_START_MISSION,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_FAILED_TO_LOAD_MISSION,
    bp.MissionState.MISSION_STATE_INACTIVE,
)
status = d.mission.get_status()
while status is None or status.state not in end_states:
    time.sleep(0.1)
    status = d.mission.get_status()
print(f"Mission ended with state {status.state.name}")

d.disconnect()
