docs.title: Blueye drone models
docs.text:
The SDK works with every Blueye model. What a script can do depends on the hardware:

Model Camera Camera tilt Guest ports CV models and laser tracking Batteries Pioneer Up to 1080p None None No 1 Pro Up to 1080p ±30° None No 1 X1 Up to 1080p ±30° 1 No 1 X3 Up to 1080p ±30° 3 No 1 X3 Ultra 4K, 60 fps up to 1440p ±30° 3 Yes 1 X7 4K, 60 fps up to 1440p ±90° 6 Yes 2

The X3 Ultra and X7 run on the NVIDIA Jetson platform. Their 4K camera has image settings, image filters and a digital pan, tilt and zoom that the older camera lacks, and no hue control. See Configure drone parameters.

docs.title: Telling the models apart from a script
docs.text:
get_model returns the model as a blueye.protocol.Model, and is_jetson_platform says whether the drone is an X3 Ultra or X7. Both read the drone's DroneInfoTel, and ask the drone for it if it has not arrived since connecting. Drone.features lists "tilt" on drones with a camera tilt. See Drone model and hardware.

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone

with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) as drone:
    if drone.get_model() == bp.Model.MODEL_X7:
        print("X7: the camera tilts ±90°")

Methods for hardware a model does not have behave in one of three ways; each method's reference says which. Some raise RuntimeError, such as the Tilt methods without "tilt" and the image filters on the older camera. Some are ignored by the drone, such as roll and pitch input on models other than the X7. Peripheral attributes such as gripper are None when no such device is attached.

docs.title: X7 notes
docs.text:
• Camera tilt. The camera tilts from -90° to +90°, and mission tilt instructions are limited to that range. enable_stabilization is accepted and is_stabilization_enabled reports it, but the tilt servo does not compensate for the drone's pitch.
  • Lights. Each side has three LEDs aimed up, ahead and down. The drone aims the light at the commanded camera tilt by dimming the LEDs that point away from it, so changing the tilt changes which lights are on.
  • Roll and pitch. The X7 is the only model that acts on roll and pitch input, see Control from a Python script.
  • Batteries. The X7 runs two batteries in parallel. get_power_source reports how the drone is powered.

docs.title: NMEA position and heading
docs.text:
This page includes example Python scripts for forwarding the drone's position and heading to NMEA receivers, and for sending an external positioning system's fixes to the drone. Each script is shown below with its filename linked to a copy bundled with this documentation version. These links also work in the SDK's installed, offline documentation.

Download all examples and extract the archive, or save the individual example and the shared nmea_utils.py helper shown at the end of this page in the same directory. Use the SDK version that matches these docs. If you need the example dependencies, install "blueye.sdk[examples]==<version>", replacing <version> with that SDK version. This keeps the SDK pinned while adding the dependencies.

The scripts use NMEA 0183 sentences with an XOR checksum (*hh) and a CRLF terminator. Coordinates are decimal degrees in Python and unsigned degrees/minutes plus hemisphere letters in the sentences.

docs.title: Forwarding the drone's position
docs.text:
The nmea_publisher.py example below subscribes to PositionEstimateTel as an observer and sends GPGLL sentences to a chart plotter or other UDP receiver. It carries the position estimate's validity flag as A (valid) or V (invalid). Non-finite or out-of-range coordinates are skipped.

The default destination is the surface-unit subnet's broadcast address, 192.168.1.255, on port 10111. Change it to your receiver's address and port. Do not broadcast these estimates to port 10110: that is the drone's position input, and feeding its output back into that input creates a feedback loop. If a chart plotter requires port 10110, send directly to the plotter's IP address.

examples/nmea_publisher.py 

"""Forward the drone's position estimate to an NMEA UDP receiver."""

import socket
import time

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone

from nmea_utils import nmea_gll

# Broadcast within the surface-unit subnet. Change this to your receiver's IP if needed.
UDP_IP = "192.168.1.255"
# Do not broadcast to 10110: the drone would consume its own position output as input.
UDP_PORT = 10111


def callback_position_estimate(
    msg_type: str, msg: bp.PositionEstimateTel, udp_socket: socket.socket
):
    """Forward each position estimate, including its validity flag."""
    position = msg.position_estimate
    try:
        sentence = nmea_gll(
            position.global_position.latitude,
            position.global_position.longitude,
            position.is_valid,
        )
    except ValueError:
        return  # No usable coordinates in this sample.
    udp_socket.sendto(sentence.encode("ascii"), (UDP_IP, UDP_PORT))
    print(f"Sent: {sentence.rstrip()}")


def main():
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as udp_socket:
        udp_socket.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
        with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) as drone:
            drone.telemetry.add_msg_callback(
                [bp.PositionEstimateTel], callback_position_estimate, udp_socket=udp_socket
            )
            try:
                while True:
                    time.sleep(1)
            except KeyboardInterrupt:
                pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Forwarding heading to a serial port
docs.text:
The nmea_heading_publisher.py example below sends the latest yaw as HDT at up to 10 Hz. Set COM_PORT and BAUD_RATE for your receiver. It connects as an observer without changing the drone-wide attitude publishing rate. It waits for an attitude message, skips non-finite values, and stops sending if no attitude has arrived for one second. Heading is wrapped and rounded to 0.0–359.9 degrees.

examples/nmea_heading_publisher.py 

"""Forward the drone's yaw as NMEA HDT to a serial port.

Install the example dependencies with: pip install 'blueye.sdk[examples]'
"""

import math
import time

import blueye.protocol as bp
import serial
from blueye.sdk import Drone

from nmea_utils import nmea_hdt

COM_PORT = "COM2"  # Change to your serial port.
BAUD_RATE = 9600
heading = math.nan
last_attitude_time = None


def callback_attitude(msg_type: str, msg: bp.AttitudeTel):
    """Keep the latest yaw and its arrival time."""
    global heading, last_attitude_time
    heading = msg.attitude.yaw
    last_attitude_time = time.monotonic()


def main():
    global heading, last_attitude_time
    heading, last_attitude_time = math.nan, None
    try:
        with serial.Serial(COM_PORT, BAUD_RATE, timeout=1) as port:
            with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) as drone:
                drone.telemetry.add_msg_callback([bp.AttitudeTel], callback_attitude)
                # Read the existing telemetry stream; do not change the rate for other clients.
                while True:
                    if last_attitude_time is not None and time.monotonic() - last_attitude_time < 1:
                        sentence = nmea_hdt(heading)
                        if sentence is not None:
                            port.write(sentence.encode("ascii"))
                            print(f"Sent: {sentence.rstrip()}")
                    time.sleep(0.1)
    except serial.SerialException as exc:
        print(f"Serial error: {exc}")
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Feeding an external position to the drone
docs.text:
The drone listens on UDP port 10110 for its own position, such as fixes from a topside USBL system. This is separate from the pilot's position. Send the ROV's measured latitude and longitude, not the boat's GPS coordinates and not the drone's own position estimate.

Blunux 4.2.6 and newer pass GNGGA, GPGLL, PBLPLL and PSONLLD sentences to the position estimator, and Blunux 5.1 adds GPGGA and GNGLL. Other sentence types are ignored. The example sends GPGLL, which all of these versions accept.

Send one checksummed, CRLF-terminated sentence per UDP datagram to the drone's IP address, normally 192.168.1.101. Supply fresh fixes at 1 Hz or faster. The NMEA navigation source expires after about three seconds without a valid fix. Mark unusable fixes invalid rather than repeatedly sending the last valid position with a new timestamp.

Position reset

The first valid NMEA fix resets the drone's local position frame and odometer. Do not inject test coordinates during a dive or a running mission.

The nmea_position_input.py example below reads latitude longitude A|V lines from standard input and unicasts a GPGLL sentence for each line. It needs no SDK connection or control of the drone. Connect it to an adapter for your positioning system that emits fresh fixes without buffering, for example:

python -u positioning_adapter.py | python examples/nmea_position_input.py --ip 192.168.1.101

positioning_adapter.py is your own adapter, not a supplied example. If it already produces NMEA, send those sentences directly instead. The supplied script does not repeat old fixes if its input stops.

examples/nmea_position_input.py 

"""Send fresh external ROV positions from stdin to the drone's NMEA UDP input.

Each line must contain: latitude longitude A|V
Coordinates are decimal degrees; A means a valid fix and V means invalid.
Supply fresh measurements at least once per second. This script sends each line
once and does not repeat old coordinates when the source stops.

Example usage with your own positioning adapter:
    python positioning_adapter.py | python examples/nmea_position_input.py --ip 192.168.1.101

The first valid fix resets the drone's local position frame and odometer.
Do not feed the boat's GPS position or the drone's own telemetry back into this input.
"""

import argparse
import socket
import sys

from nmea_utils import nmea_gll

NMEA_INPUT_PORT = 10110


def forward_positions(lines, udp_socket: socket.socket, ip: str):
    """Convert one fresh fix per line into a unicast GPGLL datagram."""
    for line_number, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        try:
            latitude, longitude, status = line.split()
            if status not in ("A", "V"):
                raise ValueError("Status must be A or V")
            sentence = nmea_gll(float(latitude), float(longitude), status == "A")
        except ValueError as exc:
            print(f"Skipping line {line_number}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
            continue
        udp_socket.sendto(sentence.encode("ascii"), (ip, NMEA_INPUT_PORT))


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--ip", default="192.168.1.101", help="Drone IPv4 address")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as udp_socket:
            forward_positions(sys.stdin, udp_socket, args.ip)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Checking that the drone receives the fixes
docs.text:
Inspect the NMEA entry in PositionEstimateTel.position_estimate.navigation_sensors. The overall estimate's is_valid flag alone does not tell you whether the NMEA source is valid.

import time

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone


def show_nmea(msg_type, msg):
    for sensor in msg.position_estimate.navigation_sensors:
        if sensor.sensor_id == bp.NavigationSensorID.NAVIGATION_SENSOR_ID_NMEA:
            print(sensor.is_valid, sensor.global_position)


with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) as drone:
    drone.telemetry.add_msg_callback([bp.PositionEstimateTel], show_nmea)
    time.sleep(10)

Older firmware may not report the per-source status. The resulting global estimate can also incorporate other sensors, so it need not equal each incoming fix exactly.

NMEA position input does not enable station keeping. See station keeping requirements and waypoint missions for supported control modes. Waypoint mission legs are limited to 300 m.

docs.title: Shared sentence formatting
docs.text:
Both position scripts and the heading publisher use this helper:

examples/nmea_utils.py 

"""NMEA sentence formatting shared by the examples in this directory."""

import datetime
import math


def nmea_sentence(body: str) -> str:
    """Add the XOR checksum and CRLF to a sentence body without delimiters."""
    checksum = 0
    for byte in body.encode("ascii"):
        checksum ^= byte
    return f"${body}*{checksum:02X}\r\n"


def _coordinate(value: float, degree_digits: int) -> str:
    # Round before splitting so 59.99996 minutes carries into the next degree.
    units = round(abs(value) * 60 * 10000)
    degrees, minute_units = divmod(units, 60 * 10000)
    minutes, fraction = divmod(minute_units, 10000)
    return f"{degrees:0{degree_digits}d}{minutes:02d}.{fraction:04d}"


def nmea_gll(lat: float, lon: float, valid: bool) -> str:
    """Format decimal-degree coordinates as GPGLL with the current UTC time.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a coordinate is non-finite or outside its geographic range.
    """
    if not math.isfinite(lat) or not -90 <= lat <= 90:
        raise ValueError("Latitude must be finite and between -90 and 90 degrees")
    if not math.isfinite(lon) or not -180 <= lon <= 180:
        raise ValueError("Longitude must be finite and between -180 and 180 degrees")
    now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
    utc_time = now.strftime("%H%M%S") + f".{now.microsecond // 10000:02d}"
    return nmea_sentence(
        f"GPGLL,{_coordinate(lat, 2)},{'N' if lat >= 0 else 'S'},"
        f"{_coordinate(lon, 3)},{'E' if lon >= 0 else 'W'},"
        f"{utc_time},{'A' if valid else 'V'}"
    )


def nmea_hdt(heading: float) -> str | None:
    """Format heading in degrees as HDT, or skip a non-finite heading."""
    if not math.isfinite(heading):
        return None
    # Wrap again after rounding: 359.99 must not be sent as 360.0.
    heading = round(heading % 360, 1) % 360
    return nmea_sentence(f"IIHDT,{heading:.1f},T")

docs.title: Odometer to Imagenex 831L Publisher
docs.text:
This example shows how one can use the blueye.sdk to forward the odometer distance from the position messages from the drone to the PipeSonarL software from Imagenex. The PipeSonarL software is used to operate the Imagenex 831L Pipe Profiling sonar.

The PipeSonarL software accepts input from external cable counting systems, which is used to generate a 3D point cloud from a pipe inspection.

On a Blueye X3, we can use the odometer distance from the position messages to generate the cable count for the PipeSonarL software. The odometer distance is the distance the drone has traveled since the last reset.

The script performs the following steps:

  1. UDP Configuration: Sets up the UDP IP and port for sending NMEA messages. If your receiver expects to receive data on a different port, you need to change it here.
  2. Increase publishing frequency: Increases the publishing frequency of the position estimate message to 5 Hz.
  3. Drone Connection: Establishes a connection to the Blueye drone.
  4. Callback Registration: Registers a callback function to handle position estimate telemetry messages.
  5. Main Loop: Keeps the script running to continuously receive and send messages.

examples/publish_odometer_to_831l.py 

"""publish_odometer_to_831l.py

This example program demonstrates how to publish the drone's odometer as a cable counter
to the PipeSonarL software used to operate the Imagenex 831L Pipe Profiling Sonar.
"""

import socket
import time

import blueye.protocol as bp

from blueye.sdk import Drone


def callback_position_estimate(
    msg_type: str, msg: bp.PositionEstimateTel, udp_socket: socket.socket
):
    """Callback for the PositionEstimateTel message."""
    odometer = msg.position_estimate.odometer * 1000  # Convert to mm
    formatted_message = f"{{,#CABLE,{odometer},mm,}}\r\n"

    udp_socket.sendto(formatted_message.encode("ascii"), (UDP_IP, UDP_PORT))
    print(f"Sent: {formatted_message.strip()}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # UDP configuration
    # This IP will broadcast to all devices in the 192.168.1 subnet
    UDP_IP = "192.168.1.255"

    # 1261 is the default UDP port used by the PipeSonarL software.
    UDP_PORT = 1261

    udp_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    udp_socket.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)  # Enable broadcasting

    # Instantiate a drone object and connect to the drone
    try:
        print("Connecting to the drone...")
        my_drone = Drone(connect_as_observer=True)
    except ConnectionError:
        print("Could not connect to the drone.")
        exit(1)
    finally:
        print("Connected to the drone.")

    # Increase publishing frequenzy for the PositionEstimateTel message
    my_drone.telemetry.set_msg_publish_frequency(bp.PositionEstimateTel, 5)

    # Add a callback for the PositionEstimateTel message
    my_drone.telemetry.add_msg_callback(
        [bp.PositionEstimateTel], callback_position_estimate, udp_socket=udp_socket
    )

    # Keep the script running to receive and send messages
    try:
        print("Press Ctrl+C to exit.")
        while True:
            time.sleep(1)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("Exiting...")
    finally:
        # Cleanup
        my_drone.disconnect()
        udp_socket.close()

docs.title: Peripherals
docs.text:
The Drone class maintains a list of peripherals that are attached to the drone. These peripherals can include cameras, grippers, and other devices that can be controlled using the drone's API.

To list the peripherals that are currently attached to the drone, you can check the peripherals attribute of the Drone class. This attribute is a list of Peripheral objects.

The SDK also has an attribute for each supported kind of peripheral (external_camera, external_light, gripper, laser, servo and skid_servo) to simplify access. If the drone carries two devices of the same kind, the attribute refers to the last one discovered; the full set is always in peripherals.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Peripherals are discovered once per connection, from the first DroneInfoTel telemetry message in which the drone lists its guest ports and the devices on them. Until then, peripherals and get_guest_ports() return None and every peripheral attribute is None; a drone that has reported but has no guest ports gives empty lists. Devices plugged in or removed later in the session are not picked up until the next connect(). Disconnecting clears the lists and the attributes.

if drone.laser is None:
    print("No scaling laser on this drone")
else:
    drone.laser.set_intensity(0.5)

Every Peripheral records which port it sits on, the interfaces it requires from that port, and which ports on the drone fully support it. For detachable devices, get_detach_status() reports whether the device is currently attached.

docs.title: Guest ports
docs.text:
To see the state of each guest port, including ports with nothing connected or with a connector fault, use get_guest_ports(). It returns one GuestPort per port the drone reports, or None if no guest port information has been received yet. A port either carries a list of devices or reports a connector error, never both; an empty port reports GUEST_PORT_ERROR_NOT_CONNECTED. Connector errors other than "not connected" are also logged as warnings when the ports are discovered.

import blueye.protocol as bp

for port in drone.get_guest_ports():
    if port.error == bp.GuestPortError.GUEST_PORT_ERROR_NOT_CONNECTED:
        print(f"{port.number.name}: empty")
    elif port.error is not None:
        print(f"{port.number.name}: connector error {port.error.name}")
    else:
        names = ", ".join(device.name for device in port.devices)
        print(f"{port.number.name}: {names}")
    print(f"  provides {[cap.name for cap in port.capabilities]}")

docs.title: Navigation sensors
docs.text:
The drone has no class for its navigation sensors yet; they appear in peripherals as plain Peripheral objects. What they provide decides which auto modes and mission instructions the drone will run:

Device Provides DVL (Water Linked A50 or A100, Nortek Nucleus, Cerulean Tracker 650) Position for station keeping, weather vaning and waypoint missions. Altitude for auto altitude and seabed-relative depth set points. Blueye GNSS Position for the same, while the drone is at the surface with a fix. Ping sonar, mounted downwards Altitude for auto altitude and seabed-relative depth set points. UGPS, USBL, NMEA input over UDP Position for the map and for waypoint missions. The drone does not hold position on these, so station keeping and weather vaning need a DVL or the Blueye GNSS as well.

PositionEstimateTel.position_estimate.navigation_sensors lists the position sensors the drone sees with an is_valid flag each, and get_altitude returns None while the altitude is not valid:

import blueye.protocol as bp
from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()

position = myDrone.telemetry.get(bp.PositionEstimateTel)
if position is not None:
    for sensor in position.position_estimate.navigation_sensors:
        print(f"{sensor.sensor_id.name}: {'valid' if sensor.is_valid else 'not valid'}")

print(f"Altitude: {myDrone.get_altitude()}")

See the movement page for the auto modes and Mission planning for the instructions.

docs.title: External camera
docs.text:
If the drone has a camera attached, the Drone class will have an external_camera attribute that is a GuestPortCamera object. This object can be used to control the camera.

# Set bitrate for external camera to 2 Mbps
drone.external_camera.set_bitrate(2_000_000)

# Start recording video from the external camera. The main camera and the multibeam keep
# whatever they were doing.
drone.external_camera.set_recording(True)

# Take a picture. The drone has one picture command for both cameras, so this captures from
# the main camera and the external camera in one go, as drone.camera.take_picture() does.
drone.external_camera.take_picture()

See Recording video and taking pictures for the details.

docs.title: External light
docs.text:
If the drone has an external light attached, the Drone class will have an external_light attribute that is a GuestPortLight object. This object can be used to control the light.

# Get the current intensity of the external light
intensity: float = drone.external_light.get_intensity()

# Set the intensity of the external light to 0.5
drone.external_light.set_intensity(0.5)

docs.title: Scaling laser
docs.text:
If the drone has a scaling laser attached (the Blueye scaling laser, the Laser Tools Sea Beam or the Spot X laser scalers), the Drone class will have a laser attribute that is a Laser object. This object can be used to control the scaling laser. The dot spacing is 50 mm for the Blueye laser and 75 mm for the Sea Beam.

# Get the current intensity of the scaling laser
intensity: float = drone.laser.get_intensity()

# Set the intensity of the scaling laser to 0.5
drone.laser.set_intensity(0.5)

docs.title: Laser dot tracking
docs.text:
On the X3 Ultra and X7 the drone can track the laser dots in the main camera image. enable_tracking modulates the laser at 5 Hz, and the drone then reports the dot positions, their distance in pixels and the estimated distance to the subject in LaserTel. The drone overwrites the modulation flag with every intensity command, so set_intensity keeps the reported flag unless you pass modulated yourself. Tracking works on the full camera image, so enable_tracking(True) also resets the digital pan, tilt and zoom to 0, as the Blueye app does.

drone.laser.enable_tracking(True)

detection = drone.laser.get_detection()  # blueye.protocol.LaserDetection, or None
if detection is not None and detection.detected:
    print(f"{detection.estimated_distance:.2f} m, dots {detection.pixel_distance:.0f} px apart")

# Or just the distance, None while the dots are not detected
print(drone.laser.get_estimated_distance())

drone.laser.enable_tracking(False)

docs.title: Gripper
docs.text:
If the drone has a gripper attached, the Drone class will have a gripper attribute that is a Gripper object. This object can be used to control the grip and rotation of the gripper.

If the connected gripper does not support rotation, the rotation velocity will be ignored.

# Open the gripper
drone.gripper.set_grip_velocity(1.0)

# Close the gripper
drone.gripper.set_grip_velocity(-1.0)

# Rotate the gripper clockwise
drone.gripper.set_rotation_velocity(1.0)

# Rotate the gripper counterclockwise
drone.gripper.set_rotation_velocity(-1.0)

docs.title: Servo
docs.text:
If the drone has a servo attached, the Drone class will either have a servo attribute that is a GenericServo object, or a skid_servo attribute that is a SkidServo object. These objects can be used to control the servo.

servo is the Blueye generic servo. It takes a position between 0 and 1, where 0 and 1 are the end stops, since the drone has no idea what that is in degrees for the servo you have fitted. The drone drives generic servos on guest ports 1 to 3 only. The old set_angle and get_angle still work but warn, they map -90..90 degrees onto the 0..1 position.

# Move to the middle
drone.servo.set_position(0.5)

# The reported position, and the position it is moving towards
drone.servo.get_position()
drone.servo.get_set_point()

With two generic servos, drone.servo is the last one discovered. Each servo in drone.peripherals reports its own port, so pick by port_number when you have more than one:

from blueye.sdk.guestport import GenericServo

servos = {p.port_number: p for p in drone.peripherals if isinstance(p, GenericServo)}

skid_servo covers every multibeam tilt servo: the skid-mounted servo (first and second generation), which tilts ±28 degrees, and the head-mounted servo, which tilts ±45 degrees. The allowed range of the connected servo is in min_angle and max_angle.

# Set the angle
drone.skid_servo.set_angle(20.0)

# Get the current angle, and the angle the servo is moving towards
drone.skid_servo.get_angle()
drone.skid_servo.get_set_point()

docs.title: Supported devices
docs.text:
Device SDK class Attribute Blueye camera GuestPortCamera external_camera Blueye light, Blueye light pair, Blue Robotics Lumen GuestPortLight external_light Blue Robotics Newton (fixed and detachable), Blueprint Lab Reach Alpha Gripper gripper Blueye scaling laser, Laser Tools Sea Beam, Spot X laser scalers Laser laser Blueye generic servo GenericServo servo Blueye multibeam servo (V1 and V2), Blueye multibeam head servo SkidServo skid_servo

Every other device the drone discovers (sonars, DVLs, GNSS, sensors, USB storage) is listed in peripherals as a plain Peripheral with its name, port and device ID, and its data is read from the matching telemetry messages through drone.telemetry.get().

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The SDK requires Python 3.10 or higher. We recommend using uv to manage your Python versions and virtual environments. uv is an extremely fast Python package installer and resolver that simplifies project setup.

The instructions below show the necessary steps to get started with the SDK on a fresh install using uv.

Windows

Install uv

Open PowerShell and run the following command to install uv: 

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Changing the execution policy allows running a script from the internet. You may need to restart your terminal for the changes to take effect.

Create a virtual environment

Using a virtual environment is highly recommended to isolate project dependencies. 

# Create a new project folder and navigate into it
mkdir drone_project
cd .\drone_project

# Create a virtual environment using Python 3.13 (uv will download it if needed)
uv venv -p 3.13
This will create a .venv folder in your project directory.

Activate the virtual environment: 

.\.venv\Scripts\activate

Install the SDK

Now we're ready to install the SDK into our active virtual environment:

uv pip install blueye.sdk

Or, to include the dependencies required for running the examples:

uv pip install "blueye.sdk[examples]"
macOS and Linux

Install uv

Open your terminal and run the following command to install uv: 

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
After installation, follow the instructions on the screen to add uv to your shell's PATH, or simply restart your terminal.

Create a virtual environment

Using a virtual environment is highly recommended to isolate project dependencies. 

# Create a new project folder and navigate into it
mkdir drone_project
cd drone_project

# Create a virtual environment using Python 3.13 (uv will download it if needed)
uv venv -p 3.13
This will create a .venv folder in your project directory.

Activate the virtual environment: 

source .venv/bin/activate

Install the SDK

Now we're ready to install the SDK into our active virtual environment:

uv pip install blueye.sdk

Or, to include the dependencies required for running the examples:

uv pip install "blueye.sdk[examples]"

docs.title: Connect to the drone
docs.text: To use the SDK, your computer must be connected to the drone via the surface unit WiFi. For instructions on how to turn on the drone and surface unit, you can watch the quick start video.

docs.title: Control the drone
docs.text:
Most of the functionality is controlled using getter and setter methods. We will illustrate their use by showing how to control the lights:

import time
from blueye.sdk import Drone

# When the Drone object is instantiated, a connection to the drone is established
myDrone = Drone()

# Setting the lights to 0.1 (10 %)
myDrone.set_lights(0.1)

time.sleep(2)

# We can also get the current brightness of the lights with the get_lights method
print(f"Current light intensity: {myDrone.get_lights()}")
myDrone.set_lights(0)

# Getter methods are also used for reading telemetry data from the drone
print(f"Current depth in meters: {myDrone.get_depth()}")
For an overview of the methods that are available for controlling and reading data from the drone, go to the Drone reference. Most functions are grouped under attributes of the Drone object, such as camera, motion, logs and telemetry; the reference lists them with links to their own pages, which give the valid input ranges.

When a script is done it should call disconnect. The drone keeps the last motion input it received until a new one arrives or its watchdog times out, so disconnect zeroes the thrusters before it tells the drone that the client is leaving. A with block does that for you, also when the script fails or is stopped with Ctrl-C, and a script that ends without either is disconnected when the interpreter exits:

from blueye.sdk import Drone

with Drone() as myDrone:
    myDrone.motion.set_surge(0.3)
    ...
# Thrusters zeroed and disconnected here

Tip

You can explore the methods of the drone interactively using an interactive Python interpreter like iPython, which can be installed with: 

uv pip install ipython
By instantiating a Drone object and using the completion key (normally the tab-key ↹), you can get an interactive list of the available methods on the drone, making it easy to try setting and getting the different values.

docs.title: Watching the video stream
docs.text:
The easiest way to open the RTSP video stream is by using VLC media player. Once VLC is downloaded, you can start the stream like this. The RTSP URL is: rtsp://192.168.1.101:8554/test

For lower latency streaming (on a PC), you can see the instructions on using Gstreamer, or if you just want to watch a low-latency stream, you can download the Blueye Observer app. (iOS / Android)

For video-only viewing alongside a controlling SDK script, use VLC or the Blueye Observer app. The normal Blueye app initially connects as an observer, but starting a dive requires control; if the SDK holds it, the app refuses to start the dive. For telemetry or log scripts alongside a pilot using the app, connect with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) so the script neither takes nor inherits control. See Connecting to the drone for connection options and control handover.

docs.title: Try the command line interface
docs.text:
The SDK also installs a blueye command for common tasks straight from the terminal — for example, grabbing the newest dive log from the drone:

blueye logs download --latest 1 --dives-only

The drone is always writing a log while it is powered on, so --latest skips that open log and --dives-only leaves out the short logs from powering the drone on at the desk.

Run blueye --help to see everything it can do, or read more on the blueye CLI page.

docs.title: Explore the examples
docs.text:
For how to move the drone, its axes, force levels and auto modes, see Control from a Python script.

Download the examples for this documentation version. The archive includes shared helpers and is also available in the SDK's installed, offline docs.

Remember to install the example dependencies before running the examples.

uv pip install "blueye.sdk[examples]"

docs.title: Local documentation
docs.text:
Since the drone surface unit (usually) does not have internet access it can be a bit tricky to reference this documentation while developing on the drone. Luckily when you install the SDK from PyPI it includes a pre-built, local copy of this documentation. This documentation can be viewed by executing the following Python snippet:

import blueye.sdk

blueye.sdk.open_local_documentation()

docs.title: Subscribing to a telemetry message
docs.text:
The drone publishes all of its telemetry data as protobuf encoded messages transmitted via a ZeroMQ socket. You can find the protobuf message definitions in the Protocol Definitions repository, and the generated python definitions are located in the blueye.protocol repository.

Upon connection the Drone object will instantiate an instance of the Telemetry class as the telemetry attribute. Using this attribute one can control various telemetry function and add/remove new callbacks.

docs.title: Adding a callback
docs.text: To add a callback we need to use the add_msg_callback function, and provide it with a list of telemetry messages types we want it to trigger on, as well as a function handle to call. All available telemetry messages can be found in telemetry.proto

docs.title: Removing a callback
docs.text: A callback is removed with remove_msg_callback using the ID returned when creating the callback.

docs.title: Adjusting the publishing frequency of a telemetry message
docs.text:
set_msg_publish_frequency changes how often the drone publishes a telemetry message. The frequency must be greater than 0 and at most 100 Hz.

The drone has a single telemetry publisher shared by every connected client, so the new rate also applies to the Blueye app and any other SDK client, and it stays in effect until the drone reboots. There is no request for restoring the default, so set the rate back yourself before your program exits if other clients depend on it, as the example at the bottom of this page does.

Not every message has a publish frequency. The messages in EVENT_DRIVEN_TELEMETRY are published when their data arrives, such as a sonar ping or a detection, rather than on a timer. Messages from peripherals, like the thickness gauge, only exist while that peripheral is connected. The drone refuses to change the frequency in both cases, and the SDK raises a RuntimeError that names the message and the reason.

On Blunux versions older than 5.1, changing a rate could stop the drone from publishing that message until it restarts, while the request still reported success. If a message goes quiet after a rate change on such a drone, a reboot brings it back.

docs.title: Adjusting the logging frequency of a telemetry message
docs.text:
The drone writes telemetry to the dive log at its own rate, separate from the publish rate. set_msg_log_frequency changes how often a message is logged, for example to get IMU or DVL data at a higher rate in the log without sending it to every client at that rate. It requires Blunux 5.1 or newer and takes the same frequency range as the publish frequency.

On the X3 Ultra and X7 a multibeam recording raises the log rate of six messages while it runs (PositionEstimateTel, AttitudeTel, CalibratedImuTel, CalibratedImuHpTel, DepthTel and AltitudeTel) and restores their defaults when it stops. A rate set for one of those is replaced both times.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following example illustrates how can use a callback to print the depth reported by the drone.

examples/print_depth.py 

"""print_depth.py

This example program demonstrates how one can add a callback function to a telemetry message, as
well as how to adjust the frequency of that telemetry message, and how to remove the callback.
"""

import time

import blueye.protocol as bp

from blueye.sdk import Drone


def callback_depth(msg_type: str, msg: bp.DepthTel):
    """Callback for the depth telemetry message

    This function is called once for every DepthTel message received by the telemetry watcher
    """
    print(f"Got a {msg_type} message with depth: {msg.depth.value:.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with Drone(connect_as_observer=True) as my_drone:
        # Add a callback for the DepthTel message, storing the ID for later use
        callback_id = my_drone.telemetry.add_msg_callback([bp.DepthTel], callback_depth)

        try:
            # This demonstration changes a drone-wide rate even though we are an observer.
            # Omit the rate changes if another client needs its current rate preserved.
            my_drone.telemetry.set_msg_publish_frequency(bp.DepthTel, 5)

            # Callback is triggered by a separate thread while we sleep here
            time.sleep(5)
        finally:
            my_drone.telemetry.remove_msg_callback(callback_id)

            # Restore the default, also on Ctrl-C. This is not necessarily the rate another
            # client had set before this example ran.
            my_drone.telemetry.set_msg_publish_frequency(bp.DepthTel, 10)

docs.title: Visualize dive log sensor data with Foxglove
docs.text:
With some simple steps you can visualize dive log data with ease in Foxglove. This is a great tool to play back and visualize control signals and estimated states and other sensor data from the dive.

  1. Download Foxglove here and create an account.
  2. Install the SDK with the cli extra to get the blueye CLI and the .mcap converter: pip install "blueye.sdk[cli]".

  3. Download the newest dive log from the drone and convert it in one step:

    blueye logs download --latest 1 --dives-only --mcap

    --latest skips the log the drone is writing right now, and --dives-only skips logs the drone did not count as dives: ones where it never went deeper than 25 cm and no auto function was used, such as a power-on at the desk.

    Already have .bez files on disk? Convert them directly — no drone needed:

    blueye logs convert mydive.bez

  4. Open Foxglove, in the top left menu, click on Open local file, and pick your newly created .mcap-file.

  5. Click on Add panel, and Raw message, or Plot and select the signal you want to display.
  6. Start typing DepthTel.depth.value to get auto-complete on all available messages in the protocol.
  7. You can also get a nice overview of the logged messages with this command: mcap info logfile.mcap in your terminal.

For programmatic access to the log records (the converter is built on the same parser), see LogStream.

docs.title: Legacy log file format
docs.text:
This page describes the legacy log file format. Blunux v3.0 introduced a new logfile format, and no longer logs telemetry in this format. See Plotting for an example on how to use the new format.

The log files from the Blueye drones are in essence a recording of the data that is published over UDP stored as a comma-separated-value (CSV) file.

The rest of this page documents the most useful fields of the log files. The column indices listed are zero-based. If you feel that some fields need more documentation, feel free to open an issue on Github, and we'll happily supply the requested information.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Column Type Unit Description 2 Integer Milliseconds The elapsed time since the start of the log 3 Float Unix timestamp Global time

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
The position is based on the user's phone's GPS at the start of the dive.

Column Type Unit Description 6 Float Degrees Latitude 7 Float Degrees Longitude

docs.title: File storage
docs.text: Column Type Unit Description 8 Integer Bytes Total file storage on the drone 9 Integer Bytes Available free space

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text:
Note: All temperatures are in "deci-degrees Celsius", ie. to get °C you need to divide the value by 10.

Column Type Unit Description 11 Integer Deci-Celsius Bottom canister temperature 12 Integer Deci-Celsius Water temperature 13 Integer Deci-Celsius Top canister temperature 14 Integer Deci-Celsius CPU temperature

docs.title: Internal humidity
docs.text:
Note: The unit is in deci-percent (ie. divide by 10 to get percent).

Column Type Unit Description 15 Integer Deci-percent Humidity in the top canister. 16 Integer Deci-percent Humidity in the bottom canister.

docs.title: Lights
docs.text: Column Type Unit Description 17 Integer - State of the on-board light. Range is 0 to 255.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text: Column Type Unit Description 22 Integer Milli-meters Depth below water surface. Positive values are below the surface, negative are above.

docs.title: Control force
docs.text:
Control force is the force exerted on the drone by the control system.

Column Type Unit Description 29 Float Newton Force in the surge direction. 30 Float Newton Force in the sway direction. 31 Float Newton Force in the heave direction. 32 Float Newton-meters Moment in the yaw direction.

docs.title: Orientation (pose)
docs.text: Column Type Unit Description 32 Float Degrees Roll angle. Range from -180° - 180° 33 Float Degrees Pitch angle. Range from -180° - 180° 34 Float Degrees Yaw angle. Range from -180° - 180°

docs.title: Battery
docs.text: Column Type Unit Description 38 Integer Milli-volts Battery voltage 39 Integer Milli-amperes Battery current. Negative values are drained from the battery, positive are charged. 41 Integer Percent Relative state of charge. Range from 0 - 100 %

docs.title: Logs from the drone
docs.text:
The drone opens a new log file every time it is powered on and writes telemetry such as depth, temperature and attitude to it until it is powered off. These files can be downloaded to your computer, where you can plot them or process them however you see fit.

Blunux 3.0 introduced a binary log format that replaced the older CSV logs. A binary log is a gzip-compressed sequence of length-prefixed BinlogRecord Protobuf messages. Each record holds a unix timestamp in UTC, the monotonic timestamp (time since boot), and an Any message wrapping a Blueye protocol message, most often a telemetry message. The telemetry messages are documented in the telemetry proto. Drones on Blunux older than 3.0 are covered at the end of this page.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
The binary logs are also available through the blueye CLI, which is installed with the SDK and connects to the drone as an observer — taking no control:

blueye logs list                       # table of logs on the drone
blueye logs download --latest 1        # newest finished log to the current directory
blueye logs download --latest 1 --mcap # ...and convert it for Foxglove
blueye logs download --latest 1 --dives-only  # newest dive, skipping power-on logs
blueye logs download BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00002 -o ~/dives
blueye logs                            # interactive: pick logs to download

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Logs are read over HTTP, so you do not need control of the drone to work with them. Connect as an observer, which leaves the pilot in control and still lets you list and download logs:

from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone(connect_as_observer=True)

The examples below use this myDrone object.

docs.title: Listing the log files
docs.text:
If your drone has completed 5 dives and you do

print(myDrone.logs)

you should see something like the following lines be printed

Name                                Time                Max depth    Size
BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00000  07. Aug 2023 12:10  7 m          217.1 KiB
BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00001  08. Aug 2023 12:35  20 m         1.6 MiB
BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00002  09. Aug 2023 14:20  100 m        3.8 MiB
BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00003  10. Aug 2023 09:15  200 m        6.5 MiB
BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00004  11. Aug 2023 15:01  300 m        10.2 MiB

The first part of the filename (the part before the _) is the serial number of your drone, the second part is the unique ID of the drone, and the third part is the log number. In addition we see the start time of the log, the maximum depth reached, and the size of the log file.

Max depth is rounded down to the nearest meter for dives up to 10 meters, rounded down to the nearest 10 meters for dives up to 100 meters, and rounded down to the nearest 100 meters for deeper dives.

The index is fetched from the drone the first time you touch myDrone.logs. To pick up logs that were created after that, refresh it:

myDrone.logs.refresh_log_index()

docs.title: What a log file knows about itself
docs.text:
Each entry in the index is a LogFile with these attributes:

Attribute Type Meaning name str The log name, as listed above, without the .bez extension. start_time datetime When the log was started, in UTC. is_dive bool True if the drone went deeper than 25 cm during the log. Depending on the Blunux version, an auto function, thruster input, a running mission or a camera or multibeam recording also counts. is_open bool True if the drone is still writing to the log. See Limits. filesize int Size of the compressed log on the drone, in bytes. max_depth_magnitude int Deepest point of the log in meters, rounded down as described above. download_url str The URL the log is downloaded from. content bytes The downloaded, still compressed, log, or None until download() has been called.

docs.title: Selecting a log file
docs.text:
There are multiple ways to select a log file from the logs index, here are some examples showing how to select by index, by name, and by slice.

By index

from blueye.sdk.logs import LogFile

first_log: LogFile = myDrone.logs[0]
last_log: LogFile = myDrone.logs[-1]

By name

from blueye.sdk.logs import LogFile

log: LogFile = myDrone.logs["BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00000"]

By slice

from blueye.sdk.logs import Logs

first_three_logs: Logs = myDrone.logs[:3]
last_three_logs: Logs = myDrone.logs[-3:]
every_other_log: Logs = myDrone.logs[::2]

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Logs.filter takes a function that gets a LogFile and returns a new Logs index with the entries the function accepted. Some examples:

dive_logs = myDrone.logs.filter(lambda log: log.is_dive)
deep_logs = myDrone.logs.filter(lambda log: log.max_depth_magnitude >= 50)
finished_logs = myDrone.logs.filter(lambda log: not log.is_open)

The filtered index can be indexed, sliced and iterated like myDrone.logs:

latest_dive = myDrone.logs.filter(lambda log: log.is_dive and not log.is_open)[-1]

docs.title: Downloading a log file to your computer
docs.text:
When you want to download a log file all you have to do is to call the download() method on the desired log and the file will be downloaded to your current folder.

Following are some examples of how one can download log files.

Downloading a single log file

The following will download the first log with its default name to the current folder: 

myDrone.logs[0].download()

If we wish to specify the name/path of the log file we can use the optional output_path parameter: 

myDrone.logs[0].download(output_path="/tmp/my_log.bez")

If output_path is a directory, the log is saved there with its default name.

Downloading multiple log files

Downloading multiple log files is solved by a simple Python for-loop. The example below shows how one can download the last 3 logs to the current folder: 

for log in myDrone.logs[-3:]:
    log.download()

Adding a prefix to log names

The example code below shows how one can add a simple prefix to all log files when downloading:

prefix = "pre_"
for log in myDrone.logs:
    log.download(output_path=prefix + log.name + ".bez")

download() keeps the downloaded bytes in log.content and returns them, so calling it again on the same LogFile does not contact the drone unless you pass overwrite_cache=True. Pass write_to_file=False to get the bytes without saving a file.

docs.title: Streaming the records
docs.text:
LogFile.parse_to_stream() downloads the log if needed and returns a LogStream, an iterator that decompresses and decodes the log one record at a time. Each record is a tuple of four values:

Position Type Meaning 0 DatetimeWithNanoseconds The drone's wall clock when the record was written, in UTC. 1 timedelta Time since the first record in the log, from the drone's monotonic clock. 2 message type The protocol class of the message, for instance bp.DepthTel. 3 message The decoded message. 
import blueye.protocol as bp

for wall_time, since_start, message_type, message in myDrone.logs[0].parse_to_stream():
    if message_type is bp.DepthTel:
        print(f"{since_start}  {message.depth.value:.2f} m")

The wall clock is only as good as the drone's clock. The drone does not keep time across power cycles; the SDK and the Blueye app set it when they take control, so the records before that carry a wrong date. The monotonic delta is always continuous. LogStream also accepts the bytes of a log that is already on disk:

from blueye.sdk.logs import LogStream

with open("BYEDP000000_ea9ac92e1817a1d4_00000.bez", "rb") as f:
    stream = LogStream(f.read())

Plotting log files shows how to load a stream into a pandas DataFrame, and the Foxglove page how to convert one for playback.

docs.title: Message types this SDK does not know
docs.text:
The drone logs every message type its firmware knows, so a drone on a newer release than your blueye.protocol package can produce records the SDK has no class for. LogStream skips those by default: the first record of each type logs a warning, and all of them are counted per type URL in stream.unknown_types. To get them anyway, pass include_unknown=True and the stream yields them as (wall_time, since_start, type_url, raw_bytes) tuples, where type_url is a string such as "type.googleapis.com/blueye.protocol.PowerCanisterTel" and raw_bytes is the undecoded payload. parse_to_stream() does not take the argument, so build the stream yourself:

from blueye.sdk.logs import LogStream

log = myDrone.logs[0]
stream = LogStream(log.download(write_to_file=False), include_unknown=True)

Upgrading blueye.protocol is the way to decode them.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One log is always open. The drone writes a new log from power-on to power-off, so the log for the current power cycle has is_open set while you are connected. The drone flushes it to disk every 10 seconds, so downloading it gives a snapshot that stops mid-record. download() warns about this and does not cache open logs. The CLI's --latest skips them.
  • Logs stop after 10 hours. The drone closes a log after 600 minutes even if it stays powered on. Nothing after that is logged until the next power cycle.
  • Logging can be switched off. The drone's storage settings in the Blueye app have a switch for the dive log ("binlog"). With it off the drone writes no log at all, so myDrone.logs shows nothing new after a dive. The same settings have switches for videos and images; set_recording and take_picture raise when the matching one is off, since the drone would drop the recording or the picture.
  • Download timeout. download(timeout=...) defaults to 1 second. This is the requests timeout: the time allowed to connect, and then between bytes, so a large log is not cut off as long as the drone keeps sending. On a slow link, raise it.
  • Index timeout. refresh_log_index(timeout=...) defaults to 10 seconds per request. Drones on Blunux older than 3.3 need one extra request per log to fill in the dive info, so the first listing on a drone with many logs takes a while.
  • Error responses raise. A requests.HTTPError is raised if the drone answers a log request with an error status, rather than saving the error page as a log.

docs.title: Legacy CSV logs (Blunux older than 3.0)
docs.text:
Drones on Blunux older than 3.0 store CSV logs instead, available as myDrone.legacy_logs. The format is described on the legacy log file format page. The index works like the binary one, with a few differences.

Listing, selecting and downloading legacy logs 
print(myDrone.legacy_logs)

Name                        Time                Max depth  Size
ea9add4d40f69d4-00000.csv   24. Oct 2018 09:40  21.05 m    6.3 MiB
ea9add4d40f69d4-00001.csv   25. Oct 2018 10:29  21.06 m    879.2 KiB
ea9add4d40f69d4-00002.csv   31. Oct 2018 10:05  60.69 m    8.5 MiB
ea9add4d40f69d4-00003.csv   31. Oct 2018 12:13  41.68 m    8.4 MiB
ea9add4d40f69d4-00004.csv   02. Nov 2018 08:59  52.52 m    7.8 MiB

The first part of the filename (the part before the -) is the unique ID of your drone and the second part is the dive number.

The drone leaves out logs with a max depth below 20 cm. To list them as well, refresh the index with get_all_logs=True:

myDrone.legacy_logs.refresh_log_index(get_all_logs=True)

Select by index, by name or by slice. Slicing a legacy index gives a list rather than a new index:

from blueye.sdk.logs import LegacyLogFile

first_log: LegacyLogFile = myDrone.legacy_logs[0]
log: LegacyLogFile = myDrone.legacy_logs["ea9add4d40f69d4-00000.csv"]
first_three_logs: list[LegacyLogFile] = myDrone.legacy_logs[:3]

download() takes output_path, the directory to save to, and output_name, the file name to use. The drone samples at 10 Hz, and downsample_divisor (default 10) picks every n-th sample:

myDrone.legacy_logs[0].download()
myDrone.legacy_logs[0].download(output_path="/tmp/", output_name="my_log.csv")

for log in myDrone.legacy_logs[-3:]:
    log.download()

prefix = "pre_"
for log in myDrone.legacy_logs:
    log.download(output_name=prefix + log.name)

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
This example shows how one can pull a log file from the drone and use pandas and matplotlib to plot it.

We'll start by picking a log file from the drone, connecting as an observer since we do not need control:

from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone(connect_as_observer=True)
log = myDrone.logs[0]

Next we'll parse the log to a stream and create a pandas dataframe from the records. We'll also specify the column names to make it easier to work with the dataframe later.

import pandas as pd
import blueye.protocol as bp

columns = ["rt", "delta", "meta", "message"]
log_stream = log.parse_to_stream()
divelog = pd.DataFrame.from_records(log_stream, columns=columns)

The four columns are the record tuple described in Streaming the records: the wall clock time, the time since the first record, the message type and the message.

We'll now filter out all entries that are not depth telemetry messages and messages that were logged before the start of the dive.

depth_log = divelog[divelog.meta == bp.DepthTel]
depth_log = depth_log[depth_log.rt > log.start_time]

We can now extract the depth value from the remaining entries

depth_log["depth"] = depth_log["message"].apply(lambda x: x.depth.value)

We'll prepare our axes for plotting

x = depth_log["rt"]
y = depth_log["depth"]

Next we will plot depth vs time with matplotlib: 

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Instantiate our figure and axes to plot on
figure, axes = plt.subplots()

# Plot the depth values against time
axes.plot(x, y, label="depth")

# Set title, labels, and legend
plt.title("Depth chart")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Depth [m]")
plt.legend()

# Save the figure
figure.savefig("depth_plot.svg")

This should yield us a plot that looks something like this:

See the matplotlib documentation for more ways to plot your data.

Blunux older than 3.0 (CSV logs)

Drones on Blunux older than 3.0 store CSV logs instead. Download one with the legacy index and read it into pandas:

from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone(connect_as_observer=True)
myDrone.legacy_logs[0].download(output_name="log0.csv")

import pandas as pd

divelog = pd.read_csv("log0.csv")

Convert the unix timestamp in rt_clock into a more readable format, and prepare the axes. Depth is logged in millimeters:

divelog["rt_clock"] = pd.to_datetime(divelog["rt_clock"], unit="s")

x = divelog["rt_clock"]
y = divelog["depth"] / 1000  # Dividing by 1000 to get depth in meters

The matplotlib part above is the same from here.

docs.title: Log statements from the blueye.sdk
docs.text:
The blueye.sdk package uses the standard Python logging module to log information about the SDK's operation. The log statements are useful for debugging and troubleshooting, and can be used to get a better understanding of what is happening inside the SDK.

Note: These logs must not be confused with the divelogs that are generated and stored on the drone. See Listing and downloading logfiles for instructions on how to get the divelogs.

Events with severity WARNING or greater are printed to sys.stderr by default, but can be configured to be written to a file or sent to a remote server. See the Python logging documentation for more information about how to configure the logging module.

The SDK logs under the blueye.sdk logger and its children, one per module, such as blueye.sdk.logs and blueye.sdk.connection. Configuring blueye.sdk covers all of them.

docs.title: Enabling logging with lower severity
docs.text:
By default, the events with severity lower than WARNING are muted. To enable them, you need to configure the logger to capture the logs. Here's an example of how to enable debug logs:

import logging
import blueye.sdk

def enable_debug_logs():
    # Set the logger configuration
    logger = logging.getLogger(blueye.sdk.__name__)
    logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

    # Define the log handler
    handler = logging.StreamHandler()
    handler.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

    # Define the log format
    formatter = logging.Formatter('%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
    handler.setFormatter(formatter)

    # Add the log handler to the logger
    logger.addHandler(handler)

In the example above, we import the necessary modules and create a function enable_debug_logs() to enable the runtime logs. We configure the logger to capture logs with the logging.getLogger(blueye.sdk.__name__) statement and set the log level to DEBUG to capture all logs.

We also define a log handler to determine where the logs should be outputted. In this example, we use a logging.StreamHandler() to print the logs to the console. You can customize the log handler based on your requirements, such as writing logs to a file or sending them to a remote server.

Finally, we set the log format using logging.Formatter() and add the log handler to the logger using logger.addHandler(handler).

docs.title: Disabling logging
docs.text:
To keep the SDK's log records out of your program's output entirely, stop them at the blueye.sdk logger:

import logging
import blueye.sdk

def disable_logging():
    logger = logging.getLogger(blueye.sdk.__name__)
    logger.addHandler(logging.NullHandler())
    logger.propagate = False

Both lines are needed. propagate = False keeps the records from reaching the root logger, which is where logging.basicConfig() or a framework would otherwise print them. The NullHandler gives the logger a handler of its own, so Python's last-resort handler does not print warnings to sys.stderr for a logger that has none. Adding a NullHandler alone does not help once the root logger is configured, since the records still propagate to it.

Setting logger.disabled = True is not enough either: it only silences the blueye.sdk logger itself, and the modules log through child loggers.

docs.title: Receiving logs in another terminal
docs.text:
Sometimes the program output can become quite cluttered if the logs are being printed in between the program output. In such cases, it can be useful to run the program in one terminal and then run a separate terminal to read the logs. This can be accomplished by configuring a simple TCP server to listen for log messages. Here's an example of how to do this:

import logging
import logging.handlers
import socketserver
import struct


class LogRecordStreamHandler(socketserver.StreamRequestHandler):
    def handle(self):
        while True:
            chunk = self.connection.recv(4)
            if len(chunk) < 4:
                break
            slen = struct.unpack(">L", chunk)[0]
            chunk = self.connection.recv(slen)
            while len(chunk) < slen:
                chunk = chunk + self.connection.recv(slen - len(chunk))
            obj = self.unPickle(chunk)
            record = logging.makeLogRecord(obj)
            self.handleLogRecord(record)

    def unPickle(self, data):
        import pickle

        return pickle.loads(data)

    def handleLogRecord(self, record):
        logger = logging.getLogger(record.name)
        logger.handle(record)


class LogRecordSocketReceiver(socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer):
    allow_reuse_address = True

    def __init__(
        self,
        host="localhost",
        port=logging.handlers.DEFAULT_TCP_LOGGING_PORT,
        handler=LogRecordStreamHandler,
    ):
        socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer.__init__(self, (host, port), handler)


logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s:\n    %(message)s\n"
)
tcpserver = LogRecordSocketReceiver()
print("Starting logging server...")
tcpserver.serve_forever()

And then we need to configure the SDKs logger to send the logs to this server.

import logging
import logging.handlers

from blueye.sdk import Drone

# Set up logging
logger = logging.getLogger("blueye.sdk")
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
socket_handler = logging.handlers.SocketHandler(
    "localhost", logging.handlers.DEFAULT_TCP_LOGGING_PORT
)
logger.addHandler(socket_handler)

d = Drone()

# Logs from the SDK will now be sent to the logging server

docs.title: Control from a Python script
docs.text:
A Drone object has a motion attribute, an instance of Motion, with the methods that move the drone and switch its auto modes on and off. Each setter gives one axis a setpoint between -1 and 1, which the drone holds until it gets a new one:

import time
from blueye.sdk import Drone

with Drone() as myDrone:
    myDrone.motion.set_surge(0.4)
    time.sleep(1)
    myDrone.motion.set_surge(0)
# Leaving the block zeroes every setpoint and disconnects

The drone drops motion input while nobody is in control, and an observer is never given control, so a script that pilots the drone should connect without connect_as_observer=True. See Connecting to the drone.

docs.title: Axes and directions
docs.text:
Axis Setter A positive setpoint Models Surge set_surge moves forward All Sway set_sway moves right All Heave set_heave moves down All Yaw set_yaw turns clockwise, seen from above All Roll set_roll rolls right X7 Pitch set_pitch raises the nose X7

Surge, sway and heave setpoints are forces. Yaw, roll and pitch setpoints are moments. The models other than the X7 ignore roll and pitch, so those setters are safe to call on any drone. On the X7, read set_roll before using them: with auto heading off nothing limits the resulting angle.

docs.title: How strong a setpoint is
docs.text:
A setpoint of ±1 is full stick. It does not ask for the most the thrusters can give: the force depends on boost and slow.

  • Normal, with boost and slow at 0, is the drone's everyday level.
  • Boost, set_boost(1), raises full stick to the drone's boosted force.
  • Slow, set_slow(1), lowers it for fine positioning.

At full stick, as a share of the boosted force, with the drone's default force settings:

Axis Normal Slow Surge 27 % 4 % Sway 39 % 13 % Heave 44 % 18 % Yaw, roll and pitch 52 % 16 %

Boost and slow each have a dead band of 0.1: values up to 0.1 count as 0, and 0.1 to 1 is stretched over the whole range, so a boost of 0.55 is halfway. The drone then takes boost minus slow and blends linearly toward the boosted level when the result is positive and toward the slow level when it is negative. Both at 1 give the normal level. A setpoint between 0 and 1 scales the force in proportion.

docs.title: One axis or all at once
docs.text:
The setters change one axis and keep the others. send_thruster_setpoint sets surge, sway, heave and yaw in one message, and roll and pitch as keyword arguments that default to 0. get_current_thruster_setpoints returns what the SDK last sent.

In a control loop, compute every axis and send them with one send_thruster_setpoint call per iteration:

import time
from blueye.sdk import Drone

with Drone() as myDrone:
    end = time.monotonic() + 5
    while time.monotonic() < end:
        # Compute every axis here, for example from a controller
        myDrone.motion.send_thruster_setpoint(surge=0.3, sway=0, heave=-0.1, yaw=0)
        time.sleep(0.05)  # 20 Hz

docs.title: Auto modes and what they need
docs.text:
The auto modes are enabled with the enable_* methods on motion. The drone checks its sensors when a mode is requested. The drone does not send a notification when it refuses a mode. It writes an error to its own log and leaves the mode off, so read the matching is_*_active() method afterwards. ControlModeTel carries the same flags.

Mode Needs When the requirement is lost Auto depth Nothing beyond the built-in depth sensor. Turns auto altitude off. Auto heading Nothing beyond the built-in IMU. Auto altitude A valid altitude from a DVL or a downward-facing Ping sonar on a guest port. Turns auto depth off. The drone switches to auto depth. Station keeping A valid position from a DVL or the drone's own Blueye GNSS. Topside positioning (UGPS, USBL, NMEA input) does not count. Released after 3 seconds without a valid position. Weather vaning The same as station keeping, which it turns on. As for station keeping.

With auto depth or auto altitude on, the heave setpoint asks for a vertical speed instead of a force, and 0 holds the depth or altitude. With auto heading on, the yaw setpoint asks for a turn rate, and 0 holds the heading.

The position sensors and their validity are listed in PositionEstimateTel.position_estimate.navigation_sensors, and get_altitude returns None while the altitude is not valid. See Navigation sensors for which guest-port devices provide what.

import time
from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()
myDrone.motion.enable_station_keeping(True)
time.sleep(1)
if not myDrone.motion.is_station_keeping_active():
    print("Station keeping did not engage: no valid DVL or GNSS position")

docs.title: Stopping safely
docs.text:
The drone keeps the last setpoint it received, so a script that stops sending does not stop the drone. Set every axis back to 0 with zero_setpoints when a manoeuvre is done. disconnect, and the end of a with block, zero the setpoints before leaving when the script is in control. When connecting, the SDK zeroes them only if it gets control.

If the client in control stops sending its watchdog for 3 seconds, the drone zeroes the input and switches the auto modes off, see Connecting to the drone.

docs.title: Controlling the drone from a gamepad
docs.text:
To run the example remember to first install the optional dependencies needed for running the examples 

pip install "blueye.sdk[examples]"

The example below illustrates how one could use an Xbox controller and the SDK to control the drone.

The inputs library supports many other gamepads, so using a different controller should be as simple as looking up the event codes for the buttons/axes and mapping them to the functions you want.

examples/gamepad_controller.py 

import inputs

from blueye.sdk import Drone


class JoystickHandler:
    """Maps drone functions to joystick events"""

    def __init__(self, drone):
        self.drone = drone
        self.event_to_function_map = {
            "BTN_NORTH": self.handle_x_button,
            "BTN_WEST": self.handle_y_button,
            "BTN_EAST": self.handle_b_button,
            "BTN_SOUTH": self.handle_a_button,
            "ABS_X": self.handle_left_x_axis,
            "ABS_Y": self.handle_left_y_axis,
            "ABS_Z": self.handle_left_trigger,
            "ABS_RX": self.handle_right_x_axis,
            "ABS_RY": self.handle_right_y_axis,
            "ABS_RZ": self.handle_right_trigger,
        }

    def handle_x_button(self, value):
        """Starts/stops the video recording"""
        self.drone.camera.set_recording(value)

    def handle_y_button(self, value):
        """Turns lights on or off"""
        if value:
            if self.drone.get_lights() > 0:
                self.drone.set_lights(0)
            else:
                self.drone.set_lights(0.1)

    def handle_b_button(self, value):
        """Toggles autoheading"""
        if value:
            self.drone.motion.enable_auto_heading(not self.drone.motion.is_auto_heading_active())

    def handle_a_button(self, value):
        """Toggles autodepth"""
        if value:
            self.drone.motion.enable_auto_depth(not self.drone.motion.is_auto_depth_active())

    def filter_and_normalize(self, value, lower=5000, upper=32768):
        """Normalizing the joystick axis range from (default) -32768<->32678 to -1<->1

        The sticks also tend to not stop at 0 when you let them go but rather some
        low value, so we'll filter those out as well.
        """
        if -lower < value < lower:
            return 0
        elif lower <= value <= upper:
            return (value - lower) / (upper - lower)
        elif -upper <= value <= -lower:
            return (value + lower) / (upper - lower)
        else:
            return 0

    def handle_left_x_axis(self, value):
        self.drone.motion.set_yaw(self.filter_and_normalize(value))

    def handle_left_y_axis(self, value):
        self.drone.motion.set_heave(self.filter_and_normalize(value))

    def handle_right_x_axis(self, value):
        self.drone.motion.set_sway(self.filter_and_normalize(value))

    def handle_right_y_axis(self, value):
        self.drone.motion.set_surge(-self.filter_and_normalize(value))

    def handle_left_trigger(self, value):
        self.drone.motion.set_slow(self.filter_and_normalize(value, lower=0, upper=255))

    def handle_right_trigger(self, value):
        self.drone.motion.set_boost(self.filter_and_normalize(value, lower=0, upper=255))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Leaving the `with` block disconnects, which zeroes the thrusters first. That holds for
    # Ctrl-C and for any exception, so the drone is never left running the last stick position.
    with Drone() as myDrone:
        handler = JoystickHandler(myDrone)
        try:
            while True:
                events = inputs.get_gamepad()
                for event in events:
                    if event.code in handler.event_to_function_map:
                        handler.event_to_function_map[event.code](event.state)
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            pass

docs.title: AnnotationCtrl
docs.text:
Request to add an annotation to the current dive.

Sent by the app when a diver picks a type from the in-dive command palette. The drone stamps the authoritative time, publishes the result as an AnnotationTel to every connected client, and writes it to the dive logfile, so all clients converge on the same set. Fire-and-forget, like LightsCtrl.

Attributes:

  • annotation (Annotation) –

    The annotation to record. The drone owns the timestamp, not this message.

docs.text:
Message sent when the user wants to set color correction settings. Applies depth- and scene-driven underwater color correction, restoring the red/blue balance lost with depth. The intensity field scales the correction (0.0 = off/identity, 1.0 = full). Only supported on X3 Ultra.

  • image_height (int) –

    Height of the frame the bounding box was drawn on.

docs.title: VisionTrackingCtrl
docs.text:
Issue a command to set the vision-based tracking mode.

Setting a mode requires an actively tracked single-object-tracking (SOT) target; the drone refuses to enable a mode otherwise. Setting a different mode while one is active switches atomically. Sending a state with no mode set disables vision tracking. An OrbitState with a zero rate is rejected.

Attributes:

  • state (VisionTrackingState) –

    The desired vision tracking mode, or none to disable.

    Message with the number of seconds the client has been connected.

  • client_id (int) –

    The ID of the client, received in the ConnectClientRep response.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
A single annotation added during a dive, e.g. by a diver tapping a type in the app command palette, or emitted by the drone itself.

Self-contained: it carries the type's display fields (name/icon/color) inline, so the drone, any connected client, and the dive logfile can render it without a separate catalog. The app keeps the full catalog locally (synced from Blueye Cloud) to drive its palette, but only complete annotations go over the wire. type_slug lets Blueye Cloud correlate the annotation to its type on import.

The drone owns the timestamp: when this is logged the enclosing BinlogRecord carries the time, like any other sample, so there is no time field here.

Attributes:

  • type_slug (str) –

    Stable type id for grouping / Cloud correlation. Empty for a free-form annotation.

  • type_name (str) –

    Type display name, e.g. "Hazard". Snapshot of the type at creation time.

  • type_icon (str) –

    Font Awesome solid icon name, kebab-case (e.g. "triangle-exclamation").

  • type_color (str) –

    Type color, RGB hex incl. leading '#', 7 chars (e.g. "#DC2626").

  • title (str) –

    Optional annotation title; Cloud falls back to type_name if empty. Max 200 chars.

  • body (str) –

    Optional free-form note. Unbounded.

  • duration (Duration) –

    Optional span; omit for a point-in-time marker.

  • source (AnnotationSource) –

    Origin of the annotation; the app sets APP, the drone sets DRONE for its own.

docs.title: LaserDetection
docs.text:
Message representing the detection of scaling lasers in the main camera. The message contains the centroids of the detected dots, the distance between them in pixels, and the confidence of the detection. The dots are detected through temporal DFT analysis of 5 Hz laser modulation, isolating flickering pixels from the static scene background.

Only available on Ultra.

Attributes:

  • detected (bool) –

    True if the laser is detected by the drone.

  • dot1 (Point2D) –

    First dot centroid (leftmost).

  • dot2 (Point2D) –

    Second dot centroid (rightmost).

  • pixel_distance (float) –

    Distance between dots in pixels.

  • confidence (float) –

    Confidence of the detection (0..1).

  • image_width (int) –

    Source frame width.

  • image_height (int) –

    Source frame height.

  • laser_width (float) –

    Real world distance between the two laser dots (m).

  • corrected_pixel_distance (float) –

    Distance after lens undistortion (px).

  • estimated_distance (float) –

    Estimated subject distance (m).

docs.title: SegmentationMask
docs.text:
RLE-encoded binary segmentation mask with its own anchor box.

The mask bitmap has dimensions (mask_width x mask_height) covering the mask_box region of the camera image. The counts field stores run-length encoded data as packed uint16 little-endian: alternating background/foreground pixel runs starting with background. Runs longer than 65535 pixels are split by inserting a zero-length run of the opposite class (e.g. 70000 becomes 65535, 0, 4465), so decoders need no special handling — a zero-length run just toggles the class.

Scale the mask to mask_box, not to the detection's bounding_box: the bounding box may be smoothed by tracking, while mask_box is pinned to the raw detection position, so the mask stays on the actual object pixels.

Attributes:

  • mask_width (int) –

    Width of the RLE bitmap.

  • mask_height (int) –

    Height of the RLE bitmap.

  • counts (bytes) –

    RLE counts as packed uint16 little-endian.

  • mask_box (BoundingBox) –

    Image region the mask bitmap covers (raw detection position, never smoothed).

docs.title: VisionTrackingState
docs.text:
The active vision-based tracking mode.

The modes are mutually exclusive, which the oneof encodes: at most one mode is set at a time, and no field set means no vision tracking mode is active.

Each mode's message documents which degrees of freedom it controls automatically; any degree of freedom not listed as automatic remains under pilot control. Pilot input on an automatically controlled degree of freedom is ignored while the mode is active.

This message has oneof_ fields (mutually exclusive fields). For each oneof, at most one member field can be set at the same time. Setting any member of the oneof automatically clears all other members.

.. _oneof: https://proto-plus-python.readthedocs.io/en/stable/fields.html#oneofs-mutually-exclusive-fields

Attributes:

  • spotlight (SpotlightState) –

    Spotlight mode is active.

    This field is a member of oneof_ mode.

  • active_track (ActiveTrackState) –

    Active track mode is active.

    This field is a member of oneof_ mode.

  • orbit (OrbitState) –

    Orbit mode is active, at the reported angular rate.

    This field is a member of oneof_ mode.
