def enable_auto_altitude(self, enable: bool):
    """Enable or disable the auto altitude control mode

    When auto altitude is active, the drone will attempt to maintain its current altitude above
    the seabed. Heave input (`set_heave` or `send_thruster_setpoint`) specifies a
    speed set point instead of a force set point. A control loop on the drone will then attempt
    to maintain the wanted speed in the heave direction as long as auto altitude is active.

    Auto altitude needs a valid altitude, which comes from a DVL or a downward-facing Ping
    sonar on a guest port. `get_altitude()` returns `None` while there is none. Without it the
    drone drops the request and only logs it on its own side, so check
    `is_auto_altitude_active()` afterwards. Enabling auto altitude turns auto depth off, also
    when the auto altitude request itself is dropped. If the altitude becomes invalid while
    auto altitude is active, the drone switches to auto depth.

    Args:
        enable (bool): Activate auto altitude mode if true, de-activate if false.
    """
    self._parent_drone._ctrl_client.set_auto_altitude_state(enable)

enable_station_keeping(enable: bool)

Enable or disable the station keeping control mode

When station keeping is active, the drone will attempt to maintain its current position and orientation in the water as long as the mode is active.

Station keeping needs a valid position from a DVL or from the drone's own Blueye GNSS. Topside positioning (UGPS, USBL or NMEA input over UDP) is used for the map position but does not count here: those fixes jump between samples, and the drone would chase every jump. Without a valid position the drone drops the request and only logs it on its own side, so check is_station_keeping_active() afterwards. An active hold is released when the position has been invalid for 3 seconds. PositionEstimateTel.position_estimate.navigation_sensors lists each sensor with its validity.

docs.title: send_thruster_setpoint
docs.text:
send_thruster_setpoint(
    surge, sway, heave, yaw, *, roll=0.0, pitch=0.0
)

Set the setpoint of every axis in one message.

Each setpoint is between -1 and 1 and scales the force (or, for yaw, roll and pitch, the moment) linearly. A setpoint of 1 or -1 is full stick, whose force depends on set_boost and set_slow, not the most the thrusters can give.

Roll and pitch are keyword-only and default to 0, so a call that leaves them out clears any roll or pitch set earlier. Only the Blueye X7 acts on them, and with auto heading off they are open-loop moments that nothing on the drone limits. See set_roll and set_pitch for how auto heading changes their meaning and why the autopilot ignores them.

Parameters:

  • surge (float) –

    Force set point in the surge direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point makes the drone move forward.

  • sway (float) –

    Force set point in the sway direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point makes the drone move to the right.

  • heave (float) –

    Force set point in the heave direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point makes the drone move down.

  • yaw (float) –

    Moment set point in the yaw direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point makes the drone rotate clockwise.

  • roll (float, default: 0.0 ) –

    Moment set point in the roll direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point rolls the drone to the right. X7 only.

  • pitch (float, default: 0.0 ) –

    Moment set point in the pitch direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point pitches the nose of the drone up. X7 only.

def send_thruster_setpoint(self, surge, sway, heave, yaw, *, roll=0.0, pitch=0.0):
    """Set the setpoint of every axis in one message.

    Each setpoint is between -1 and 1 and scales the force (or, for yaw, roll and pitch, the
    moment) linearly. A setpoint of 1 or -1 is full stick, whose force depends on
    [`set_boost`][blueye.sdk.motion.Motion.set_boost] and
    [`set_slow`][blueye.sdk.motion.Motion.set_slow], not the most the thrusters can give.

    Roll and pitch are keyword-only and default to 0, so a call that leaves them out clears any
    roll or pitch set earlier. Only the Blueye X7 acts on them, and with auto heading off they
    are open-loop moments that nothing on the drone limits. See `set_roll` and `set_pitch` for
    how auto heading changes their meaning and why the autopilot ignores them.

    Args:
        surge (float): Force set point in the surge direction in range <-1, 1>,
                       a positive set point makes the drone move forward.
        sway (float): Force set point in the sway direction in range <-1, 1>,
                      a positive set point makes the drone move to the right.
        heave (float): Force set point in the heave direction in range <-1, 1>,
                       a positive set point makes the drone move down.
        yaw (float): Moment set point in the yaw direction in range <-1, 1>,
                     a positive set point makes the drone rotate clockwise.
        roll (float): Moment set point in the roll direction in range <-1, 1>,
                      a positive set point rolls the drone to the right. X7 only.
        pitch (float): Moment set point in the pitch direction in range <-1, 1>,
                       a positive set point pitches the nose of the drone up. X7 only.
    """
    with self.thruster_lock:
        self._current_thruster_setpoints["surge"] = surge
        self._current_thruster_setpoints["sway"] = sway
        self._current_thruster_setpoints["heave"] = heave
        self._current_thruster_setpoints["yaw"] = yaw
        self._current_thruster_setpoints["roll"] = roll
        self._current_thruster_setpoints["pitch"] = pitch
        self._send_motion_input_message()

docs.title: set_pitch
docs.text:
set_pitch(pitch_value: float)

Set moment reference for the pitch direction

Only the Blueye X7 has thrusters that can produce a pitch moment. Other models ignore this input.

With auto heading off the value is an open-loop moment set point, like yaw, and nothing on the drone limits the resulting angle. The drone settles where the thruster moment is balanced by its righting moment, and a large input held for a few seconds can tip it over. The drone keeps acting on the last setpoint for as long as the SDK is connected, so set it back to 0 when the manoeuvre is done.

With auto heading on the drone instead holds a pitch angle. The value is then an angular speed set point for that angle, which is bounded to 45 degrees either side of level, and the drone keeps the angle it has reached when the input returns to 0. Engaging auto heading resets the held roll and pitch angles to level.

While the autopilot is running a mission the drone holds level and ignores pitch input. Starting the autopilot also switches auto heading off.

Parameters:

  • pitch_value (float) –

    Moment set point in the pitch direction in range <-1, 1>, a positive set point pitches the nose of the drone up.

def describe_enum(value) -> str:
    """Render a protocol enum value for a log or error message.

    A drone running a newer Blunux than the SDK can report an enum value this build does not
    know, and proto-plus surfaces those as a plain int rather than an enum member. Fall back to
    `UNKNOWN(<number>)` so the message still says which value was received.
    """
    return getattr(value, "name", f"UNKNOWN({value})")

def deserialize_any_to_message(msg: Any) -> Tuple[type, proto.message.Message]:
    """Deserialize a protobuf Any message to a concrete message type.

    Args:
        msg (Any): The Any message to deserialize. Needs to be a message defined in the
                   blueye.protocol package, a well-known wrapper type (FloatValue, Int32Value,
                   etc) from google.protobuf.wrappers_pb2, or google.protobuf.Empty.

    Returns:
        A tuple with the message type and the deserialized message. blueye.protocol types
        come back as proto-plus messages, the google.protobuf types as plain protobuf messages.

    Raises:
        UnknownMessageTypeError: The type URL names a type this SDK does not have a class for.
    """
    type_url = msg.type_url
    google_prefix = "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf."
    blueye_prefix = "type.googleapis.com/blueye.protocol."
    if type_url == google_prefix + "Empty":
        return (empty_pb2.Empty, empty_pb2.Empty.FromString(msg.value))
    if type_url.startswith(google_prefix):
        payload_type = getattr(wrappers, type_url[len(google_prefix) :], None)
        if payload_type is None:
            raise UnknownMessageTypeError(type_url)
        return (payload_type, payload_type.FromString(msg.value))
    if type_url.startswith(blueye_prefix):
        payload_type = getattr(bp, type_url[len(blueye_prefix) :], None)
        if payload_type is not None:
            return (payload_type, payload_type.deserialize(msg.value))
    raise UnknownMessageTypeError(type_url)

def is_scalar_type(msg: proto.message.Message) -> bool:
    """Check if a message is a scalar type

    Args:
        msg (proto.message.Message): The message to check

    Returns:
        True if the message is a scalar type, False otherwise
    """

    scalar_types = (
        FloatValue,
        Int32Value,
        Int64Value,
        UInt32Value,
        UInt64Value,
        DoubleValue,
        BoolValue,
        StringValue,
        BytesValue,
    )
    return isinstance(msg, scalar_types)

    sdk_path = os.path.dirname(blueye.sdk.__file__)

    # The documentation is located next to the top-level package so we move up a couple of levels
    documentation_path = os.path.abspath(sdk_path + "/../../blueye.sdk_docs/index.html")

    webbrowser.open(documentation_path)

docs.title: Camera calibration
docs.text:
The X3 Ultra and X7 publish the intrinsic calibration of the main camera as part of the DroneInfoTel telemetry message. The calibration uses the pinhole camera model with OpenCV distortion coefficients (k1, k2, p1, p2, k3), which is what the Blueye app uses to undistort the video.

The SDK exposes it through Camera.get_calibration, which returns a CameraCalibration message, or None if the drone has not published one. Older models (Pioneer, Pro, X1 and X3) and the guestport camera do not publish a calibration.

from blueye.sdk import Drone

drone = Drone()

calibration = drone.camera.get_calibration()
if calibration is None:
    print("The connected drone does not publish a camera calibration")
else:
    print(f"Calibrated at {calibration.image_width}x{calibration.image_height}")
    print(f"fx={calibration.fx:.1f} fy={calibration.fy:.1f} "
          f"cx={calibration.cx:.1f} cy={calibration.cy:.1f}")
    print(f"Distortion: {list(calibration.distortion_coefficients)}")
    if calibration.is_default:
        print("This is the built-in default for the model, not a per-drone calibration")

docs.title: Scaling to the video resolution
docs.text:
The focal lengths and principal point are in pixels at the resolution the calibration was computed at. Before using them on a frame of a different size they have to be scaled: fx and cx with the width ratio, fy and cy with the height ratio. The distortion coefficients are resolution independent.

Camera.get_scaled_calibration does this for you. Without arguments it scales to the current stream resolution, and it also accepts a Resolution or a (width, height) tuple. A Resolution maps to the frame size the drone's video pipeline produces for it, which is 640x480 for 480p and 16:9 for the other resolutions.

import blueye.protocol as bp

# Matches the frames you receive from the RTSP stream
calibration = drone.camera.get_scaled_calibration()

# Matches a recording made at 4K
calibration = drone.camera.get_scaled_calibration(bp.Resolution.RESOLUTION_UHD_4K)

# Matches a frame you have already resized
calibration = drone.camera.get_scaled_calibration((640, 360))

docs.title: Undistorting a frame with OpenCV
docs.text:
The message maps directly onto the arguments OpenCV expects.

import cv2
import numpy as np

calibration = drone.camera.get_scaled_calibration((frame.shape[1], frame.shape[0]))

camera_matrix = np.array([
    [calibration.fx, 0.0, calibration.cx],
    [0.0, calibration.fy, calibration.cy],
    [0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
])
distortion = np.array(calibration.distortion_coefficients)

undistorted = cv2.undistort(frame, camera_matrix, distortion)

docs.title: Older models
docs.text:
Drones that do not publish a calibration have to be calibrated by hand, for example with OpenCV's chessboard calibration. As a starting point, Johan Kvalberg measured the following values for a Blueye Pioneer in his master thesis. The thesis does not state the image resolution the values were computed at, and the camera, housing and water all affect the result, so treat them as an example rather than a calibration of your drone.

import numpy as np

# Blueye Pioneer, in water
camera_matrix = np.array([
    [1354.45761, 0.0, 891.069717],
    [0.0, 1379.97405, 756.192877],
    [0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
])
distortion = np.array([-0.2708139, 0.20052465, 0.0208302, 0.0002806, -0.10134601])

# Blueye Pioneer, in air
camera_matrix_air = np.array([
    [978.36617202, 0.0, 985.08473535],
    [0.0, 975.69987506, 541.52130078],
    [0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
])
distortion_air = np.array([-0.37370139, 0.26899755, -0.00120655, -0.00185788, -0.1411856])

docs.title: Downloading videos and images
docs.text:
Videos and images can easiest be downloaded through the mobile app, or by using the Blueye file transfer desktop application for Windows, Mac OS and Linux.

If one wants a more control over the download process, all files are listable through any client that supports WebDAV. The server is available on the drone (default ip: 192.168.1.101) and port 5050.

For example using a Python WebDAV client we could do the following to list the files on drone:

import webdav3.client as wc

# Define the options for connecting
options = {
    'webdav_hostname': "http://192.168.1.101:5050"
}

# Instantiate the connection
client = wc.Client(options)

# List the avaiable files
client.list()

docs.title: Understanding the file name formats
docs.text:
An example output from listing available files could be:

'video_BYEDP000105_2019-08-13_103035.jpg'
'video_BYEDP000105_2019-08-13_103035.mp4'
'picture_BYEDP000105_2019-09-27_074152.431.jpg',
The format of the file names are described below.

docs.title: Video files
docs.text:
For each video recorded on the drone two files will be created, a .mp4 file with the actual video, and a .jpg file with a thumbnail image from the video file. Other than the file extension the file names will be identical. An example of a video + thumbnail pair could be: 

'video_BYEDP000105_2019-08-13_103035.jpg'
'video_BYEDP000105_2019-08-13_103035.mp4'
The file names break down to:

File Type Prefix Drone Serial Number Timestamp (yyyy-MM-dd_hhmmss) File Extension video BYEDP000105 2019-08-13_103035 .mp4 video BYEDP000105 2019-08-13_103035 .jpg

docs.title: Image files
docs.text:
Image files are images captured with the still image function. The file name for image files follow the same format as the video files, but the time stamp is extended with milliseconds to differentiate still images captured within the same second.

An example still image file could be:

'picture_BYEDP000105_2019-09-27_074152.431.jpg',
The file name breaks down to:

File Type Prefix Drone Serial Number Timestamp (yyyy-MM-dd_hhmmss.SSS) File Extension picture BYEDP000105 2019-09-27_074152.431 .jpg

docs.title: GStreamer for video streaming
docs.text: GStreamer is the lowest latency alternative for streaming video from the drone to your laptop.

docs.title: Installing GStreamer
docs.text:
To run the streaming pipeline in the next section you will need a runtime installation of GStreamer. The instructions below show the basic steps for installing GStreamer on the most common operating systems. You can find more in depth instruction for your specific operating system in the GStreamer docs.

Windows

On Windows the basic installation steps are:

  1. Download the relevant installer for your computer from https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/download . Using the latest stable relase should be fine, at the time of writing that is 1.16.1 runtime installer
  2. Run the installer. When asked to choose a setup type choose to do a complete installation. This is because some plugins that are needed for the basic pipeline later are not included if you choose to install the typical setup
  3. To run GStreamer commands form the terminal, GStreamer must be added to the PATH environment variable. This can be done from the advanced system settings. Add %GSTREAMER_1_0_ROOT_X86_64%\bin to path. Alternatively you can choose to run gst-launch-1.0.exe from the folder it is installed in, typically C:\gstreamer\1.0\x86_64\bin
Mac OS

On Mac OS GStreamer and its plugins can be installed using brew 

brew install gstreamer gst-plugins-base gst-plugins-good gst-plugins-bad gst-plugins-ugly gst-libav

Linux

On Ubuntu and Debian GStreamer and its plugins can be installed using apt. 

apt-get install libgstreamer1.0-0 gstreamer1.0-plugins-base gstreamer1.0-plugins-good \
gstreamer1.0-plugins-bad gstreamer1.0-plugins-ugly gstreamer1.0-libav gstreamer1.0-doc \
gstreamer1.0-tools gstreamer1.0-x gstreamer1.0-alsa

You can test the installation by trying the basic pipeline from the next section when connected to a drone. Or with

gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc ! autovideosink

docs.title: Basic streaming pipeline
docs.text:
After installing you can run this pipeline in your terminal:

Windows 
gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location=rtsp://192.168.1.101:8554/test latency=0 ! rtph264depay ! avdec_h264 ! videoconvert ! fpsdisplaysink sync=false
Linux and macOS 
gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location=rtsp://192.168.1.101:8554/test latency=0 \
    ! rtph264depay \
    ! avdec_h264 \
    ! videoconvert \
    ! fpsdisplaysink sync=false

Running the pipeline will open a window with the camera stream and information about packet loss and camera frame rate.

docs.title: External camera streaming pipeline
docs.text:
If you have a X3 drone with an external camera connected you can use the following pipeline:

Windows 
gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location=rtsp://192.168.1.101:8555/guestport_cam latency=0 ! rtph264depay ! avdec_h264 ! videoconvert ! autovideosink sync=false
Linux and macOS 
gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location=rtsp://192.168.1.101:8555/guestport_cam latency=0 \
    ! rtph264depay \
    ! avdec_h264 \
    ! videoconvert \
    ! autovideosink sync=false

Running the pipeline will open a window with the external camera stream.

docs.title: Recording video and taking pictures
docs.text: The drone records video and stores pictures on its own storage. This page covers starting and stopping a recording, taking a still, what the drone does with each command, and what can keep it from recording. Downloading videos and images covers getting the files off the drone afterwards.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
import time

from blueye.sdk import Drone

myDrone = Drone()

try:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 15
    while not myDrone.camera.is_recording_active():
        if time.monotonic() >= deadline:
            raise TimeoutError("The camera did not start recording")
        myDrone.camera.set_recording(True)
        time.sleep(1)

    time.sleep(10)
    print(f"Recording: {myDrone.camera.is_recording_active()}, {myDrone.camera.get_record_time()} s")
finally:
    myDrone.camera.set_recording(False)

set_recording starts or stops the main camera. The same methods on external_camera do the same for a guest port camera. The drone has one record command for all of its recorders: the main camera, the guest port camera and the multibeam. The SDK fills in the current state of the recorders you are not changing from the latest RecordStateTel, which the drone publishes twice a second by default, so a recording started from the Blueye app keeps running when a script starts or stops another one. A recording that started after the last report can be missed, from another client or from your own previous call. When starting more than one recorder, wait until is_recording_active confirms the first before starting the next.

set_recording needs that telemetry to have arrived. Right after connecting it may not have, in which case the call logs a warning and sends nothing. is_recording_active returns None in the same case.

The camera service needs watchdog messages from a client in control before it accepts a recording start. The sender of the recording command can be an observer if another client holds control. After connecting or taking control, allow time for the watchdog and recording telemetry to arrive; the example retries for up to 15 seconds and checks that recording has started. An RTSP viewer is not required. The X3 Ultra's camera service has a 60-second timeout for stopping an ongoing recording without a control watchdog. See Connecting to the drone for how control is assigned.

get_record_time is the length of the current recording in seconds, and -1 while not recording.

docs.title: Resolution, frame rate, codec and bitrate
docs.text: On Blunux 4.4.1 and newer the recording and the live stream have separate resolutions: set_recording_resolution and set_recording_codec apply to the file, set_stream_resolution and set_bitrate to the stream, and set_framerate sets the camera's frame rate. set_recording_bitrate needs Blunux 5.0.0. On older Blunux the two share one resolution. See Configure drone parameters for the ranges per model.

docs.title: Taking pictures
docs.text:
myDrone.camera.take_picture()

take_picture requests a still picture to be stored on the drone. The picture command has no camera selector: the drone forwards the request to the main camera and, if a guest port camera is attached, to that camera too. myDrone.external_camera.take_picture() sends the same command. The app's Internal / External / Both camera setting applies to video recording, not this picture command. Mission camera instructions capture from the main camera only.

Pictures get EXIF GPS tags when the drone has a position. set_bitrate_still_picture sets the bitrate of the still picture stream they are taken from.

docs.title: Storage settings
docs.text: The drone's storage settings in the Blueye app have switches for videos, images, the multibeam and the dive log. With videos off the drone never starts a recording, and with images off it drops the picture, in both cases without a word to the client. set_recording(True) and take_picture() raise RuntimeError when the matching switch is off. The SDK reads the switches when it connects, and reads them again before refusing, so a switch turned on after connecting is picked up; a switch turned off after connecting is not, and the command is sent as before. Wrapping the request that changes the settings is tracked in #252.
